static.welcome_body:
You just did something most people never do. You took the time to look inward. That’s not a small thing. Whether you’re here because a coach recommended this, a colleague forwarded it, or you simply got curious and we’re glad you showed up!

What you’re holding is a hypothesis about your personality — specifically, a map of what drives you, how you see the world, and why you do the things you do. It’s built from how you responded to the InsightOut Assessment, and it’s designed to be a starting point, not a final word.

This report is organized as a journey: first, a brief introduction to the Enneagram system itself, then a deep dive into the pattern your responses point to most strongly. Along the way we’ll also introduce a secondary hypothesis — another pattern worth exploring with a coach.

There’s no perfect outcome here. The goal isn’t to be “typed correctly” — it’s to see yourself a little more clearly, and to have a richer conversation with whoever helps you go deeper.

We hope it lands!

You are the final authority on your own type. If something in here resonates deeply, wonderful — that’s the recognition we’re going for. If something doesn’t quite fit, that’s useful information too. Hold all of it lightly, and stay curious.

primer.intro:
The Enneagram is a dynamic system that describes nine distinct ways of being in the world — nine strategies, shaped early in life, for how to get what we need, stay safe, and belong. Each type is anchored by a core worldview and a deep motivational drive that shapes everything: how we think, what we feel, and how we act.

Understanding your type isn’t about putting yourself in a box. It’s about seeing the pattern clearly enough that you have a choice about it.
primer.scan_line: As you read, notice which descriptions pull at you — even slightly. That’s the Enneagram beginning to work.

pillars.title: Dynamic
pillars.body: A map of how you move, not just where you sit.

pillars.title: Motivational
pillars.body: Driven by your deeper “why”, not just what you do.

pillars.title: Relational
pillars.body: A lens to see yourself and everyone around you.

nine_types.name: The Protector
nine_types.description: Sees a world where only the strong protect the weak. Motivated to assert strength and guard against injustice. Attention goes to power dynamics and who needs protecting.

nine_types.name: The Giver
nine_types.description: Sees a world where love is earned through service. Motivated to be needed and seen as caring. Attention goes to others’ needs and relationship dynamics.

nine_types.name: The Observer
nine_types.description: Sees a world that is overwhelming and intrusive. Motivated to be competent and self-sufficient. Attention goes to ideas, concepts, and conserving energy.

nine_types.name: The Improver
nine_types.description: Sees a world that falls short of what it could be. Motivated to be good, principled, and beyond criticism. Attention goes to what’s wrong or is broken.

nine_types.name: The Individualist
nine_types.description: Sees a world with infinite depth but always something missing. Motivated to be authentic and deeply known. Attention goes to what’s absent or lacking.

nine_types.name: The Enthusiast
nine_types.description: Sees a world full of possibility, threatened by limitation and pain. Motivated to stay free and experience life fully. Attention goes to options and what’s next.

nine_types.name: The Peacemaker
nine_types.description: Sees a world with underlying unity that conflict threatens. Motivated to maintain harmony and avoid disconnection. Attention goes to others’ perspectives and seeking common ground.

nine_types.name: The Performer
nine_types.description: Sees a world that rewards results. Motivated to achieve and be recognized as valuable. Attention goes to goals, image, and how others perceive them.

nine_types.name: The Questioner
nine_types.description: Sees a world that is unpredictable and unsafe. Motivated by security, trust, and preparedness. Attention goes to potential threats and who can be counted on.

primer.footer: We each have access to all Enneagram types AND one of these nine patterns is your home base. Keep reading to find out which type your responses pointed to most clearly.

static.wings_primer: Wings are the two types adjacent to your core type. They flavor how your core pattern shows up — not changing who you are, but adding texture. Most people lean toward one wing; some experience both equally.
static.lines_primer: Each type has two resource points connected by lines on the diagram. Your stress point is the type your energy moves toward under pressure — often showing up as uncharacteristic behavior. Your security point is where you go when you feel safe and in flow. Awareness of these movements gives you choice about how to work with them.
static.instinct_primer: Alongside your core type, you have a dominant instinct — one of three innate drives that shape where your survival energy goes first. All three instincts are present in everyone, but one tends to run the show. Understanding your dominant instinct helps explain why two people of the same type can look quite different in practice.

instinct_definitions.name: Self-Preservation
instinct_definitions.body: Focused on safety, comfort, health, and the practical resources of daily life. SP energy goes toward securing what you need — physically, materially, and in terms of personal wellbeing.

instinct_definitions.name: Social
instinct_definitions.body: Focused on belonging, group dynamics, and your place within a community. SO energy goes toward alliances, fairness, collective causes, and knowing where you stand in relation to others.

instinct_definitions.name: One-to-One
instinct_definitions.body: Focused on deep, intense connection with specific people or experiences. SX energy goes toward chemistry, magnetism, and the quality of individual bonds — what makes a person or experience come alive.

type_8.name: The Protector

description.worldview: Eights experience the world as a place where power matters and the strong too often take advantage of the weak. Being direct, strong, and in control is how you protect yourself, the people you care about, and what you believe is right.
description.core_motivation: To be strong, stay in control of their own lives, and protect themselves and the people they love from being taken advantage of.

thinking.intro: For Eights, attention moves fast — to power, fairness, and who's doing what to whom. The mind is a rapid threat-and-opportunity scanner, wired to assess and act before others have finished thinking.
bullets: Attention goes first to power dynamics — who has it, who's misusing it, and whether things are being handled honestly.
Situations get sized up quickly — moving toward action before others have finished assessing.
Thinking runs in terms of truth and impact, with less patience for nuance that feels like hedging.
Decisiveness is real — and over time can shade into black-and-white thinking that misses complexity.
The big-picture focus is a strength — and can mean slower, smaller considerations get less attention.
There's often a strong internal sense of what's right, and a low tolerance for stories that seem designed to obscure it.
thinking.inquiry: Where does your attention go first when you walk into a room?

feeling.intro: Eights access anger quickly — it's close to the surface and reliable. Underneath it are softer feelings that take more work to reach: vulnerability, hurt, fear, tenderness.
bullets: Anger arrives first — as the immediate response to frustration, injustice, or threat. It's energizing, not shameful.
Softer feelings — hurt, fear, vulnerability — get pushed down because they feel more dangerous than the heat.
Intensity can mask how much you feel. Eights often feel more deeply than the people around them realize.
The protective drive and the tender heart are not opposites — but they rarely get equal airtime.
Tenderness shows up sideways — through protection and action more than through softness or disclosure.
The work isn't to feel less — it's to let softer feelings exist alongside the strong ones, not behind them.
feeling.inquiry: What feelings do you notice most easily — and which ones take longer to reach?

behaving.intro: Eights tend to be direct, high-energy, and forward-moving. Behavior is decisive — sometimes to the point of making others feel run over. You take charge when no one else will.
bullets: Behavior is decisive — you act when others are still thinking, and lead when no one has stepped up.
A strong protective instinct shows up in action — moving toward people or situations where strength is needed.
The shadow is excess — too much intensity, pushing past the point where others can still stay with you.
The cost shows up in relationships — people who feel loved by you and also, at times, run over by you.
Directness is a default: the hard truth gets said when the room is dancing around it.
There's often a gap between the impact you have and the impact you intend — the energy carries further than you realize.
behaving.inquiry: When do you notice the gap between how you land and how you meant to show up?

wing_a.body:
The Seven wing brings enthusiasm, appetite, and forward-moving energy into the Eight. Where the core Eight is driven by power and justice, the Seven wing adds pleasure-seeking and optimism — an instinct toward possibility and momentum. Eights with a Seven wing tend to be entrepreneurial and bold, quick to initiate and hard to slow down.

At their best: powerful and life-loving — people who lead with energy and bring others along for the ride.

wing_b.body:
The Nine wing brings calm, groundedness, and steady presence into the Eight. Where the core Eight moves fast and takes up space, the Nine wing softens the edges — producing someone who is powerful without being constantly in motion. There's more patience, more comfort with stillness.

At their best: strong and steady — power that's felt without needing to announce itself.

stress.narrative: Under significant pressure, Eights can shift toward Five energy — becoming more withdrawn, cerebral, and detached. The usual forward-moving force goes quiet; instead there's retreat into the mind and a preference for observation over action. Noticed early, it's a signal to slow down and tend to what's happening underneath.
stress.resource_card: Under pressure: withdrawal, detachment, retreat into the mind. Consciously accessed: strategic thinking, careful observation, the ability to step back before acting.

security.narrative: When Eights feel genuinely safe and resourced, they move toward Two energy — becoming warmer, more openly caring, and more willing to tend to others without the armor on. The strength is still there, but it expresses itself through generosity and attunement rather than force.
security.resource_card: In flow: warmth, care, genuine attunement. Available now: letting strength express itself through generosity rather than force.

strengths.title: Strength and Courage
strengths.body: A natural ability to take action when others hesitate — directness, decisiveness, and a willingness to confront what the room avoids.

strengths.title: Fierce Protectiveness
strengths.body: Deep loyalty to people and values — an instinct to shield those who can't protect themselves and to stand for what's right even at personal cost.

strengths.title: Honesty and Impact
strengths.body: An aversion to pretense and performance — you tell the truth, say the hard thing, and create conditions where things can actually get real.

challenges.title: Intensity That Closes Space
challenges.body: Your energy can overwhelm conversations that need to stay open — making it hard for others to bring what they're carrying without feeling run over.

challenges.title: Overriding Vulnerability
challenges.body: A habit of pushing past your own softer feelings — and sometimes others' — in the name of strength. The cost is a wall around the parts of you that are also real.

challenges.title: Impatience and Impulsiveness
challenges.body: Acting before the situation is fully understood — moving to action when more information or more time would have produced a better outcome.

practices.intro: These practices can help you build on what's already working and work with the patterns that can hold you back.
bullets: Notice the impulse to act before you act. A breath or a count to ten isn't weakness — it's choosing the response instead of running on it.
When anger or intense energy arrives quickly, get curious about what's underneath. Eights often use anger to cover softer feelings — hurt, fear, disappointment — that are harder to access.
Investigate the difference between weakness and vulnerability. Vulnerability is the capacity to be affected — not the same as being powerless. Strength and tenderness can live in the same body.
Notice the impact of your intensity on others — not to shrink it, but to choose when to bring its full force and when to bring something softer.
Practice being less certain. Be open to the possibility that someone else's perspective — especially when it contradicts yours — might contain a truth worth hearing.

communication.subhead: Communication Style — Direct, Bold, and Impact-First
bullets: You lead with your position — clear, direct, and immediately oriented to what matters. People know where you stand.
You move conversations forward. You're impatient with hedging, circling, or prolonged process when the answer seems obvious.
Your body language and tone carry weight — even when your words are measured, the intensity comes through.
You tend to speak in conclusions. The reasoning behind them is often clear to you but may not land unless you share the path, not just the destination.
watch_for: Others may hear certainty as closure — your directness can signal that the conversation is over before they've had a chance to contribute.
Intensity is a default setting — the volume you experience as normal may land louder than you intend.
Slowing down slightly, asking before stating, creates room for others to bring something you might not have considered.
Naming your intent upfront (“I want to think this through with you, not just tell you what I think”) lowers the temperature before you've even started.

conflict.subhead: Conflict Style — Into the Fire — Intensity
bullets: Conflict is not something to manage or avoid — it's information. When something is wrong, you move toward it.
You feel most alive and functional when things are real and in the open. Unresolved tension in a room is more uncomfortable to you than the confrontation itself.
The conflict response is often immediate — before others have processed that there's a conflict at all.
You have a high tolerance for rupture, and a genuine belief that things can be repaired after a hard conversation. Not everyone shares that confidence.
working_with: Not everyone in the Intensity triad is an Eight. Fours and Sixes share this response. What varies is the target: Eights move toward injustice, Fours toward meaning, Sixes toward threat.
The cost of always going in is that not all conflicts want full force. Sometimes presence and patience is enough.
After the conflict, check in. Others may still be processing what you've already moved past.
The question worth sitting with: am I moving toward this because it needs addressing, or because the tension itself is uncomfortable for me?

center.subhead: Coming Back to Center — The Body Knows First
bullets: As a Body Center type, your gut is your primary instrument — it registers threat, injustice, and opportunity before your thinking mind catches up.
This is a real intelligence, not just instinct. The gut-sense that something is off — or right — is often accurate. Trust it.
The Body Center's organizing emotion is anger. For Eights, anger is close to the surface and energizing. It rarely disappears; it transforms.
The goal isn't to stop leading with the gut — it's to stay in contact with it consciously, rather than letting it drive on autopilot.
off_center: Signals: heightened intensity, moving fast without full awareness, a sense that the room is moving too slowly or that others aren't getting it.
The return path: physical first. Slow the body down — a breath, a walk, a moment of stillness. The gut recalibrates faster when the body follows.
Access softness intentionally. Moving toward your security point (Type 2) means letting warmth and care be visible.
Notice when the intensity is covering something softer. That noticing — even briefly — is what changes the dynamic.

comparison.core_motivation: To be strong, stay in control, and protect themselves and others from being taken advantage of.
comparison.focus: Power dynamics — who has it, who's misusing it, whether things are fair and direct.
comparison.energy: Taking charge, protecting others, confronting injustice, moving from gut instinct to action.
comparison.gifts: Decisive, courageous, protective, honest, direct, energizing to be around.
comparison.challenges: Overwhelming intensity, overriding vulnerability, impulsive action, difficulty slowing down.

subtype_sp8.name: Self-Preservation Eight
subtype_sp8.tagline: The Survivalist — protective energy turned inward, building a fortress and a circle
subtype_sp8.narrative:
Self-Preservation Eights focus their protective energy on survival and territory — home, resources, and the people inside their close circle. There's often a preoccupation with having what you need: security, independence, and control over your own environment. The Eight's power goes into building and maintaining a domain that others can't easily penetrate or disrupt.

Of the three Eight subtypes, SP Eights tend to be the most contained — observing situations before moving, reading dynamics carefully, and acting when the moment is right. Relationships tend to be “in or out,” with fierce loyalty to those inside and real wariness toward those outside. The intensity is there; it's just channeled into protection rather than open display.

thinking: Attention goes to resources and territory — who controls what, whether the environment is secure, where the vulnerabilities are.
Strategic and patient before acting and moves when the moment is right.
Protects their inner circle and any thread to it activates the full Eight response immediately.
feeling: Anger is present but more contained and they are less likely to erupt publicly when a line is crossed.
Vulnerability is tightly guarded but shared more freely once trust has been built.
Tenderness is reserved for their inner circle and can be fierce and genuine.
behaving: Quiet, strategic, and observational in new situations — sizes things up before engaging.
Protective of home, resources, and the people inside the circle; territorial when those are threatened.
Can appear reserved or self-contained like Type 5 — until a line is crossed.

shifts: The classic Eight boldness is still there — but it shows up in service of building and protecting, not in constant assertion.
You may be the Eight others don't immediately recognize as one. The intensity is real; it's just more carefully managed.
The circle is small by choice, not by limitation. Loyalty runs deep; entry is earned.

subtype_so8.name: Social Eight
subtype_so8.tagline: The Group Leader — power in service of a cause, loyalty as identity
subtype_so8.narrative:
Social Eights redirect Eight energy outward — toward a group, a cause, or a fight that matters. They take a leadership role on behalf of those who can’t protect themselves, and their loyalty to people and principles runs deep. What drives this is a felt sense of moral weight as opposed to altruism.

The Social Eight is the countertype of Type 8, which means the classic confrontational, dominating image fits less cleanly here. The anger is organized around the group’s welfare, not personal power, and the force is directed outward toward injustice. This can make Social Eights read more like a Type Two or Type Six from the outside.

thinking: Attention lands on group dynamics first — who has power, who’s being marginalized, where the system is failing people.
Strategic about choosing fights; they pick their spots carefully.
Loyalty to the group creates blind spots and can obscure where people fall short in their eyes.
feeling: Anger at injustice is the primary fuel — organized around the group’s welfare, not personal grievance.
The forgiveness/justice tension is real and recurring. The pull toward accountability can be hard to release.
Tenderness is reserved and flows outward towards a small, trusted inner circle.
behaving: Leads naturally in group settings. Empowers others, organizes toward a goal, confronts unjust authority directly.
Occurs as principle-driven rather than power-driven, obscuring typical Type 8 tendencies.
Personal needs tend to go unattended and less energy goes to intimacy.

shifts: The Eight's protective instinct becomes collective — you fight for the group, the cause, or the principle, not just for yourself.
You may be the Eight who's easiest to underestimate: collaborative, friendly, principle-organized. The full force is there when the cause needs it.
The personal tends to come second. The people on your short list may feel both fiercely loved and, at times, eclipsed by the mission.

subtype_sx8.name: One-to-One Eight
subtype_sx8.tagline: The Director — intensity channeled into deep connection, provocation as contact
subtype_sx8.narrative:
One-to-One Eights have big, outgoing energy that seeks full engagement. Their force goes into significant relationships — the people they are most alive with, most in conflict with, and most protective of. Where the Social Eight fights for the group and the SP Eight protects the territory, the SX Eight wants complete connection: to know and be known, to push and be pushed back.

There’s a paradox at the heart of this subtype. The SX Eight projects enormous force — commanding, rebellious, possessive — but underneath is a longing to surrender, to trust completely, to find someone who can hold their full force without flinching. What’s easy to miss is the yearning underneath — rarely visible, rarely expressed.

thinking: Attention focuses on the significant other — their loyalty and the intensity of the connection.
Highly attuned to power within relationships: who’s giving, who’s withholding, whether the connection is real or performed.
Provocation can be intentional — testing others’ capacity to be with their big energy and power.
feeling: Emotional intensity is the most available of all three Eight subtypes; it's raw, immediate, hard to contain.
A longing to surrender runs underneath the force, to reclaim a sense of childlike innocence.
Possessiveness and protectiveness for those closest to you feels natural and necessary.
behaving: Provocative, magnetic, and bold in one-to-one contact, pushing at limits to find where the real person is.
Intensity in relationships can be electrifying and overwhelming and you need others who can match it.

shifts: The Eight's intensity concentrates into connection — it's not about the group or the territory, it's about this person, right now, fully.
The provocative edge isn't cruelty — it's contact. You push to find out who's actually there, not to drive people away.
The growing edge is surrender: trusting that allowing yourself to be held won't cost you the strength you've built.

type_9.name: The Peacemaker

description.worldview: Nines experience the world as a place that asks them to blend in and keep the peace in order to belong. Staying connected, comfortable, and harmonious feels safer than asserting a separate self that might create conflict or disruption.
description.core_motivation: To maintain inner and outer peace, stay connected to others, and avoid the conflict and discomfort that come with asserting their own priorities.

thinking.intro: For Nines, attention spreads outward to everyone else's positions, agendas, and comfort — often more readily than to their own. The mind merges with the surrounding field, which makes seeing your own stance the harder task.
bullets: Attention goes to others' agendas and to keeping the peace — your own position can be the last thing that comes into focus.
Decisions can feel hard because every side has merit; seeing all perspectives makes choosing one uncomfortable.
The mind tends to diffuse into comfortable routines and side-tasks rather than the one thing that matters most.
Knowing what you don't want is often clearer than knowing what you do — the “yes” takes more work to locate.
Mental merging means you can absorb others' opinions so thoroughly they start to feel like your own.
When pushed to assert, a quiet stubbornness can appear — a holding-the-line that surprises people who expected easy agreement.
thinking.inquiry: When you set everyone else's preferences aside, what do you actually want?

feeling.intro: Nines often experience a steady, even temperament — but the calm surface can sit on top of feelings that have been smoothed over rather than felt. Anger, in particular, tends to go underground.
bullets: Anger is the hardest feeling to access — it threatens connection, so it gets numbed before it's fully felt.
The emotional baseline is even and agreeable; strong feeling can seem like a disruption to be managed.
Discomfort gets soothed through comfort and routine rather than addressed directly.
Self-forgetting is emotional too — your own feelings can be the ones that get least attention.
When anger does surface, it can come out sideways: passive resistance, withdrawal, or a sudden immovable “no.”
Underneath the calm is a real tenderness and care — the feeling is there; the work is staying with it.
feeling.inquiry: What do you do with anger when it shows up — and where does it go?

behaving.intro: Nines tend to be easygoing, accommodating, and steady. Behavior is often organized around not making waves — going along, smoothing things over, and keeping the field comfortable for everyone.
bullets: Accommodating by default — going along with others' plans is easier than asserting your own.
Energy can diffuse into secondary tasks and comforts, while the essential thing gets postponed.
Conflict gets avoided or defused; the instinct is to lower tension, not raise it.
Stubbornness is the quiet flip side — when pushed too hard, you dig in and go immovable.
Inertia can build: starting is hard, and so is stopping once a routine is in motion.
Your steady presence is genuinely calming — people relax around you, which is a real gift and sometimes a hiding place.
behaving.inquiry: Where in your life are you going along with something you haven't actually chosen?

What do you do with anger when it shows up — and where does it go?

wing_a.body:
The Eight wing brings strength, directness, and access to anger into the Nine. Where the core Nine smooths and accommodates, the Eight wing adds backbone — more willingness to assert, to take up space, and to act on a position once it's found. Nines with an Eight wing can be more forceful and grounded than the easygoing image suggests.

At their best: peaceful and powerful — calm presence with the capacity to stand firm.

wing_b.body:
The One wing brings structure, principle, and an eye for what's right into the Nine. Where the core Nine merges and adapts, the One wing adds discernment and standards — a quieter sense of how things should be done. Nines with a One wing tend to be more orderly, idealistic, and reform-minded.

At their best: principled and accepting — steady values held without rigidity.

stress.narrative: Under significant pressure, Nines can shift toward Six energy — becoming more anxious, doubting, and worst-case-focused. The easy calm gives way to worry and a search for what could go wrong. Noticed early, it's a signal that something important has been pushed down and needs attention.
stress.resource_card: Under pressure: anxiety, doubt, scanning for what could go wrong. Consciously accessed: useful vigilance, commitment, and loyalty to what matters.

security.narrative: When Nines feel genuinely safe and supported, they move toward Three energy — becoming more focused, energized, and able to act on their own goals. The diffusion gives way to direction; priorities come into focus and get pursued.
security.resource_card: In flow: focus, drive, and the ability to act on your own priorities. Available now: stepping into your own goals rather than deferring to others'.

strengths.title: Steady Calm
strengths.body: A grounded, even presence that puts others at ease — the person who lowers the temperature in a room rather than raising it.

strengths.title: Genuine Acceptance
strengths.body: An ability to see and hold many perspectives without judgment — making others feel heard, included, and understood.

strengths.title: Natural Mediation
strengths.body: A gift for finding common ground and helping people in conflict feel that their positions matter — bridging differences others can't.

challenges.title: Self-Forgetting
challenges.body: Your own priorities, opinions, and needs can fade into the background — so far that even you lose track of what you actually want.

challenges.title: Conflict Avoidance
challenges.body: Smoothing things over can leave real issues unaddressed — and the peace you keep on the outside can cost you peace on the inside.

challenges.title: Inertia and Indecision
challenges.body: Difficulty starting, choosing, and prioritizing — energy diffuses into comfort and routine while the important thing waits.

practices.intro: These practices can help you build on what's already working and work with the patterns that can hold you back.
bullets: Practice locating your own position before you ask for everyone else's. Even a small, private “I want…” builds the muscle of knowing your own mind.
Notice when you're soothing discomfort with routine, food, or distraction instead of addressing what's actually bothering you.
Treat anger as information, not a threat to connection. The thing that irritates you is often pointing at a priority you've set aside.
Pick the one essential thing before the day diffuses into secondary tasks. Doing the important thing first protects it from inertia.
Let yourself matter in the room. Your presence is felt whether or not you assert — choosing to show up directly is a gift, not a disruption.

communication.subhead: Communication Style — Easygoing, Inclusive, and Diffuse
bullets: You communicate warmth and acceptance — people feel heard and unjudged in your presence.
You tend to see and voice multiple sides, which makes you a natural bridge but can blur where you actually stand.
You may soften or delay your own opinion to keep the conversation comfortable.
Your storytelling can wander — context and tangents come before the point, which sometimes gets lost.
watch_for: Others may not know what you think, because you've prioritized harmony over stating your view.
Saying “I don't mind” too often trains people to stop asking what you want.
Naming your position early — before you've smoothed it into everyone else's — gives the room something real to work with.
Your “yes” means more when people know you'll also say “no.” Letting disagreement show builds trust, not conflict.

conflict.subhead: Conflict Style — Around the Edges — Keeping the Peace
bullets: Conflict feels like a threat to connection, so the instinct is to lower the tension rather than enter it.
You may go along on the surface while quietly disengaging underneath — agreement that isn't fully agreement.
Direct confrontation is uncomfortable; you'd rather find the angle where everyone can be okay.
When pushed too hard, the accommodation can flip into immovable stubbornness — a quiet refusal to budge.
working_with: Avoiding conflict doesn't make it disappear — it stores it. The unaddressed thing usually resurfaces, larger.
Your stubbornness is often misread anger. Noticing it is a doorway to the position you haven't voiced.
Small, early disagreements are easier than large, late ones. Speaking up sooner keeps the peace you actually want.
The question worth sitting with: am I keeping the peace, or just keeping quiet?

center.subhead: Coming Back to Center — Coming Back Into Your Own Body
bullets: As a Body Center type, your knowing lives in the gut — but for Nines, that signal is often numbed before it registers.
The Body Center's organizing emotion is anger, and for Nines it's the most submerged. Reconnecting with it is reconnecting with your own priorities.
Presence, for you, means showing up as a distinct self — not merging into the field around you.
The goal isn't to become forceful; it's to stop disappearing — to take up the space that's already yours.
off_center: Signals: going along, diffusing into busywork, a vague sense of absence or 'checking out' of your own life.
The return path: physical and direct. Movement, a clear small action, asking yourself “what do I want” wakes the body up.
Notice numbing in real time — the second helping, the extra episode, the easy yes. That's the pattern, gently visible.
Moving toward your security point (Type 3) means letting yourself want something and act on it.

comparison.core_motivation: To keep inner and outer peace, stay connected, and avoid conflict and disruption.
comparison.focus: Others' agendas and comfort, common ground, sources of tension to be smoothed.
comparison.energy: Accommodating, mediating, maintaining harmony and routine, merging with the field.
comparison.gifts: Calm, accepting, inclusive, steady, a natural peacemaker and bridge-builder.
comparison.challenges: Self-forgetting, conflict-avoidant, indecisive, prone to inertia and stubbornness.

subtype_sp9.name: Self-Preservation Nine
subtype_sp9.tagline: The Collector — peace through comfort, routine, and the familiar
subtype_sp9.narrative:
Self-Preservation Nines create the practical rhythms and comforts that make daily life feel safe and settled. Peace comes through the body and the environment — good food, familiar routines, a comfortable space, the satisfying accumulation of things that soothe. There can be a tendency to narcotizing through habit and consumption.

Of the three Nine subtypes, SP Nines are the least visibly “peacemaking“ in the social sense — they keep the peace through their own routines rather than by managing groups or merging with a partner. This can read as self-sufficiency or contentment rather than conflict-avoidance, which is why SP Nines are sometimes the hardest Nines to spot.

thinking: Attention goes to comfort and routine — what’s familiar, what’s soothing, and what brings calm.
Practical and concrete; abstract priorities replaced by what's right in front of them.
The essential task can get crowded out by comfortable, non-essential "busy-ness".
feeling: The emotional baseline is steady and content — strong feeling gets smoothed over \[through habit.\].
Anger and discontent are numbed early, often through the body before they’re fully felt.
Underneath the calm can be resistance to anything that disrupts the familiar.
behaving: Builds and protects comfortable routines; resists disruption to the established rhythm of life.
Self-sufficient and grounded, masking an avoidance of conflict or what’s uncomfortable.

shifts: The peacemaking is private — you keep your own peace through comfort and routine more than by managing others.
You may not look like a classic Nine at all: more self-contained, more grounded, less obviously accommodating.
The growing edge is noticing the numbing — the comfortable habits that quietly substitute for what actually matters.

subtype_so9.name: Social Nine
subtype_so9.tagline: The Community Benefactor — peace through participation and belonging
subtype_so9.narrative:
Social Nines blend with the style and agenda of their groups, working hard on behalf of the collective as a way of belonging. They are often the most visibly “peacemaking“ Nines — mediating, including, showing up for the group’s harmony. Real generosity sits alongside a tendency to merge with the group and lose oneself.

Underneath the engaged, agreeable exterior is a quiet ambivalence about belonging, a longing to be fully part of the group paired with an uncertainty about whether they truly do belong. The hard work can look like earning one's place, and the inner question of do I fit in? rarely surfaces.

thinking: Attention goes to the group’s agenda and harmony — reading the collective mood, finding where things align.
Sees all sides in group dynamics and can sacrifice their own stance to preserve the peace.
The question of belonging runs underneath: am I truly part of this group?
feeling: Warm and inclusive toward the group, with a genuine care for collective wellbeing.
Personal feelings merge with the group’s mood or atmosphere.
A quiet ambivalence about belonging can sit beneath the engaged, agreeable surface.
behaving: Works hard on behalf of groups and causes — organizing, mediating, contributing selflessly.
Blends with the group’s style and agenda, losing track of one's own perspective.
Can “fall asleep“ in a comfortable social role, mistaking participation for genuine belonging.

shifts: The peacemaking goes outward — you keep harmony in groups and work hard for the collective good.
You can look highly social and engaged, which masks the inner uncertainty about whether you really belong.
The growing edge is noticing the gap between your outward agreeableness and your inner experience of belonging.

subtype_sx9.name: One-to-One Nine
subtype_sx9.tagline: The Seeker — peace through merging with a beloved other
subtype_sx9.narrative:
One-to-One Nines find peace through deep union — merging with an intimate partner, with nature, or with something larger than themselves. The longing is for fusion: to dissolve the separateness that feels lonely and to lose oneself in connection.

SX Nines can look intensely devoted, even consumed by their most important relationship — which doesn’t match the classic easygoing Nine image. They may be mistaken for Fours (in the longing) or Twos (in the merging). The self-forgetting happens through the beloved: their own desires dissolve into the other’s, and boundaries are genuinely hard to hold.

thinking: Attention orients around the beloved other; their moods and presence become the organizing center.
Their own priorities can dissolve into the relationship and become hard to recall.
Boundaries are conceptually unclear: where I end and you begin is a real, lived question.
feeling: Feelings flow through the connection - alive and full in union, lost in its absence.
A deep longing for merging underlies the relationship, and can be more intense than it appears.
Anger and personal desires are subordinated to avoid potential conflict.
behaving: Merges with the significant other, adopting their interests, rhythms, and even their opinions.
Devotion can look obsessive or all-consuming, organized entirely around the bond.
Routines, friendships, and goals get de-prioritized in favor of the beloved's.

shifts: The peacemaking happens through union — you find calm by merging deeply rather than by managing conflict.
You may look more intense and devoted than the classic Nine — closer to a Four or Two on the surface.
The growing edge is locating yourself inside the relationship: your own priorities, distinct from the beloved's.

type_1.name: The Improver

description.worldview: Ones experience the world as a place that could and should be better — where there's a right way to do things and a responsibility to live up to it. Being good, correct, and improving things is how you earn worth and avoid the sting of being wrong or bad.
description.core_motivation: To be good, right, and beyond criticism — improving themselves and the world, and living according to an inner standard of how things should be.

thinking.intro: For Ones, attention goes to what's wrong and how it could be made right. The mind runs a constant comparison between how things are and how they should be — quick to spot errors, including its own.
bullets: Attention goes straight to the flaw — the error, the gap, the thing that isn't right yet.
Thinking is organized around standards: there's a correct way, and deviations register immediately.
The inner critic runs continuously, applying the same exacting standard inward as outward.
Right and wrong feel clear and binary; gray areas and “good enough” create real discomfort.
Improvement is the default mental mode — even good things get scanned for what could be better.
There's often a sense of personal responsibility for getting it right that others don't seem to share.
thinking.inquiry: What does your inner critic say — and whose voice is it using?

feeling.intro: Ones often experience a tight, contained relationship with feeling — especially anger, which the standard says should be controlled. The result is a quiet pressure that builds beneath a composed surface.
bullets: Anger is the core feeling — but it's judged as “bad,” so it gets suppressed and leaks out as irritation, tension, or resentment.
Feelings get filtered through should: which ones are acceptable to have, and which need controlling.
The body often holds the suppressed charge — tension, tightness, a clenched quality.
Resentment builds quietly — at others who don't try as hard, and at the self for never quite measuring up.
Self-criticism can be relentless; warmth toward the self is harder to access than warmth toward others.
Underneath the control is a real longing for ease — permission to be imperfect and still be okay.
feeling.inquiry: Where do you feel the held tension in your body when something isn't right?

behaving.intro: Ones tend to be conscientious, organized, and reliable. Behavior is shaped by the standard — doing things properly, correcting what's wrong, and holding the line on quality even when others have let it slide.
bullets: Conscientious and thorough — you do things the right way, and finishing properly matters more than finishing fast.
Quick to correct and improve — pointing out errors, fixing what's off, raising the standard.
Self-discipline is high; you hold yourself to rules you'd never impose on others as harshly.
Restraint is the public face — the irritation gets controlled, which can read as stiffness or coolness.
Procrastination can appear where the standard feels unreachable — better not to start than to do it badly.
Reliability is real and deep: when you commit, it gets done, and done well.
behaving.inquiry: What would you do differently if “good enough” were actually enough?

inquiry_lines: What does your inner critic say — and whose voice is it using?
Where do you feel the held tension in your body when something isn't right?
What would you do differently if “good enough” were actually enough?

wing_a.body:
The Nine wing brings calm, patience, and a wider perspective into the One. Where the core One sharpens and corrects, the Nine wing softens — adding tolerance, ease, and a capacity to let some things go. Ones with a Nine wing tend to be more relaxed, idealistic, and measured in how they express their standards.

At their best: principled and serene — high standards held with a light hand.

wing_b.body:
The Two wing brings warmth, relationship, and a people-focus into the One. Where the core One focuses on principles and correctness, the Two wing adds care and helpfulness — directing the improving energy toward people. Ones with a Two wing tend to be warmer, more involved, and more oriented toward helping others get it right.

At their best: principled and warm — high standards in service of people.

stress.narrative: Under significant pressure, Ones can shift toward Four energy — becoming more emotional, melancholic, and focused on what's missing. The composed surface cracks, and feelings that were held down come flooding up, often with a sense of being uniquely flawed or hard done by. Noticed early, it's a signal that the suppression has reached its limit.
stress.resource_card: Under pressure: melancholy, emotional flooding, focus on what's lacking. Consciously accessed: emotional depth, authenticity, and creative self-expression.

security.narrative: When Ones feel genuinely safe and resourced, they move toward Seven energy — becoming more spontaneous, playful, and open to possibility. The grip of the standard loosens; there's more room for pleasure, fun, and doing things imperfectly just because they're enjoyable.
security.resource_card: In flow: spontaneity, playfulness, openness to pleasure. Available now: letting things be enjoyable and imperfect rather than correct.

strengths.title: Integrity and Principle
strengths.body: A deep commitment to doing what's right — honest, ethical, and reliable in ways others come to depend on.

strengths.title: Conscientious Excellence
strengths.body: High standards and the discipline to meet them — thorough, careful work that holds up under scrutiny.

strengths.title: Discernment
strengths.body: A clear eye for quality and what could be improved — the ability to see how things should be and move them toward it.

challenges.title: The Relentless Critic
challenges.body: An inner standard so exacting that nothing — including yourself — quite measures up, producing chronic self-criticism.

challenges.title: Suppressed Anger
challenges.body: Anger judged as unacceptable doesn't disappear; it leaks out as irritation, tension, and resentment.

challenges.title: Rigidity
challenges.body: Difficulty with gray areas, flexibility, and “good enough” — the right way can become the only way.

practices.intro: These practices can help you build on what's already working and work with the patterns that can hold you back.
bullets: Notice the inner critic as a voice, not a fact. You can hear it without obeying it — and ask whether its standard is actually yours.
Let anger be information. The irritation is pointing at something that matters; suppressing it just sends it underground.
Practice “good enough” on purpose. Choose something low-stakes and deliberately leave it imperfect — and notice you're still okay.
Cultivate warmth toward yourself. The standard you'd never impose on a friend is the one you apply to yourself daily.
Make room for pleasure that has no purpose. Moving toward your security point (Type 7) means letting things be fun, not just correct.

communication.subhead: Communication Style — Precise, Principled, and Correcting
bullets: You communicate clearly and precisely — accurate, well-organized, and attentive to getting the details right.
You naturally point toward improvement: what could be better, what isn't quite right yet.
Your standards come through in your tone, even when you don't state them outright.
You tend to hold back the irritation, which can read as cool, formal, or restrained.
watch_for: Constant correction, however accurate, can land as criticism — people hear the flaw before the appreciation.
Leading with what's wrong before what's working can deflate the people you're trying to help.
Naming the standard explicitly (“here's what I'm aiming for”) helps others meet it without feeling judged.
Letting some warmth and approval through — not just the correction — makes the feedback land better.

conflict.subhead: Conflict Style — By the Book — Staying Correct
bullets: Conflict gets approached through the lens of right and wrong — who's correct, what the principle is, what should have happened.
You stay composed and controlled, keeping the anger in check even when it's running hot underneath.
You'd rather resolve through reason and standards than through raw emotion.
Resentment can build silently when others don't meet the standard, surfacing later as cold irritation.
working_with: Being right and being effective aren't the same — winning the principle can lose the relationship.
The suppressed anger is felt by others even when unspoken; naming it directly is cleaner than letting it leak.
Not every disagreement has a correct answer — some are just differences in preference or perspective.
The question worth sitting with: am I trying to fix this, or to be vindicated?

center.subhead: Coming Back to Center — Releasing the Grip
bullets: As a Body Center type, your knowing lives in the gut — but for Ones it arrives pre-filtered through the standard of what's correct.
The Body Center's organizing emotion is anger, and for Ones it's controlled and judged rather than expressed.
Presence, for you, means loosening the grip — letting the body relax out of its habitual tension.
The goal isn't to abandon your standards; it's to hold them without the clench, with more ease and less self-attack.
off_center: Signals: physical tension, irritation, a tightening of the jaw or gut, the critic getting louder.
The return path: release the body first. Breath, movement, and deliberate relaxation soften the grip the mind can't.
Notice the should in real time — “I should…,” “they should…” — and ask whether it's serving you.
Moving toward your security point (Type 7) means letting pleasure and play back in, no justification required.

comparison.core_motivation: To be good, right, and beyond reproach — improving the self and the world toward an inner standard.
comparison.focus: Errors and flaws, the gap between what is and what should be, the correct way to do things.
comparison.energy: Correcting, improving, doing things properly, holding the line on quality and principle.
comparison.gifts: Principled, conscientious, honest, reliable, discerning, committed to excellence.
comparison.challenges: Self-critical, rigid, resentful, prone to suppressed anger and difficulty with 'good enough.'

subtype_sp1.name: Self-Preservation One
subtype_sp1.tagline: The Organizer — standards turned toward security and the practical world
subtype_sp1.narrative:
Self-Preservation Ones channel their standards into the practical infrastructure of life — home, work, finances, food, the physical environment. There's often an anxious edge to the pursuit of order, as if getting it right is what keeps survival secure. This is the most worried and self-controlled of the One subtypes, holding themselves to the standard most rigorously of all.

SP Ones can present as careful, contained, and worried rather than openly critical. They may not voice the standard at all — they just live by it, often at the cost of real physical tension and private resentment. This can look like generalized anxiety or conscientiousness rather than the perfectionistic structure underneath.

thinking: Attention goes to getting the practical details right — order, preparation, doing things properly.
An anxious undercurrent runs through the planning: what if it's not right, not enough, not secure?
The standard is applied most rigorously to themselves, often silently.
feeling: Worry is close to the surface — a careful, contained anxiety about getting things right.
Anger is the most suppressed of the One subtypes, held tightly and often turned inward.
Private resentment builds at carrying the standard alone while others seem more relaxed.
behaving: Meticulous about practical matters — organized, prepared, attentive to the right way of doing daily things.
Self-controlled and contained; the criticism is more often lived than spoken.
Carries visible physical tension — the suppressed charge held in the body.

shifts: The standard turns toward security and the practical world — order as a kind of safety.
You may look more worried and self-contained than openly critical — the perfectionism lives inward.
The growing edge is noticing the tension you carry and the resentment of holding the standard alone.

subtype_so1.name: Social One
subtype_so1.tagline: The Social Reformer — standards turned toward how the world should work
subtype_so1.narrative:
Social Ones channel their standards into the larger world — institutions, rules, social movements, the right way for a group or society to function. They carry a clear sense of how things should be done and a responsibility to model and advance it. They are often civic-minded, principled, and engaged, holding themselves up as an example of the correct way.

The challenge here is the difficulty flexing around others’ “incorrect“ words and actions. SO Ones can come across as principled and reform-minded rather than rigid, but the friction shows up clearly when someone doesn’t meet the standard they hold for the group.

thinking: Attention goes to how systems and groups should work - rules, structures, and standards.
Holds a clear sense of the right way for the group to do things.
Measures self and others against the social standard, and notices divergence quickly.
feeling: Carries a sense of responsibility for the group getting it right and gets frustrated when the group gets it wrong.
Anger surfaces as principled indignation about how things ought to be done.
Can feel righteous certainty and resentment for having to be the standard-bearer.
behaving: Models the correct behavior and advocates for it — civic-minded, engaged, reform-oriented.
Has difficulty adapting to others’ approaches if they don't exactly align to their standards.
Leads by example, modeling the right way of doing things.

shifts: The standard turns outward toward systems and society — how the group, the institution, the world should work.
You may read as principled and civic-minded rather than personally critical — the reform impulse is real.
The growing edge is the inadaptability: noticing how hard it is to flex around others' 'incorrect' ways.

subtype_sx1.name: One-to-One One
subtype_sx1.tagline: The Evangelist — standards charged with intensity and conviction (countertype)
subtype_sx1.narrative:
One-to-One Ones carry a charged, zealous energy just beneath a controlled surface. Their standards fuel intensity — strong convictions about how things and people should be, and real passion directed at what matters most to them, often a partner or a cause. The drive to perfect turns outward onto others rather than inward on the self.

This is the countertype within Type 1, and it can look surprisingly intense — even confrontational — which is why SX Ones are often mistaken for Eights. The controlled, quiet, self-contained image of the classic One doesn't fit here. The inner critic turns outward, producing direct challenges and strong opinions that don't look like ordinary perfectionism. The intensity is the tell.

thinking: Attention goes to perfecting the other - a partner, a cause, the right way for those close to them.
Holds intense convictions and is quick to advocate for them.
The inner critic turns outward in service to reforming others.
feeling: Anger is closer to the surface than in other Ones - charged, passionate, and confrontational.
Strong conviction and zeal reinforce their standards.
Underneath the intensity is the same longing to do the right things the right way.
behaving: Direct and forceful in advocating for their standards - can come across as Eight-like.
Pushes others to improve, with a heat typical Ones keep contained.
Channels the reforming energy into a person or cause they care about.

shifts: The standard charges outward with intensity — directed at a partner or a cause rather than held quietly inside.
You may be mistaken for an Eight: forceful, confrontational, anything but the contained classic One.
The growing edge is noticing where the perfecting energy turns onto others, and what it's really seeking.

type_2.name: The Giver

description.worldview: Twos experience the world as a place where love and belonging are earned through being needed. Attending to others, sensing what they want, and making yourself indispensable is how you secure connection and avoid the fear of being unwanted.
description.core_motivation: To be loved and needed — earning connection by giving, helping, and meeting others' needs, often before tending to their own.

thinking.intro: For Twos, attention goes outward to other people — their needs, moods, and feelings, often picked up before they're spoken. The mind is tuned to what others want and how to provide it.
bullets: Attention goes to others' needs and feelings — often sensed before the other person has named them.
Thinking is relational: situations get read through who needs what and how to help.
Your own needs can be the blind spot — harder to locate than anyone else's.
Pride can show up as the belief that you know what others need better than they do.
The mind adjusts your self-presentation to fit what each relationship seems to want.
There's often a quiet ledger running — what you've given, and whether it's been returned.
thinking.inquiry: When you stop tracking what others need, what do you notice you need?

feeling.intro: Twos live close to feeling — warm, expressive, and attuned to the emotional currents around them. The harder edge is that their own difficult feelings, especially need, get pushed out of view.
bullets: Warmth and care flow easily; the heart is open and emotionally responsive to others.
Your own needs and hurt are the hardest feelings to acknowledge — admitting them feels like weakness.
Feelings can shift to match the relationship, mirroring what the other person seems to want.
Underneath the giving can be unspoken hurt when the care isn't noticed or returned.
Pride resists receiving — being the helper feels safer than being the one who needs help.
The real longing is to be loved for yourself, not just for what you provide.
feeling.inquiry: What feelings do you tend to hide because they feel too needy to show?

behaving.intro: Twos tend to be helpful, generous, and warm — moving toward people, anticipating needs, and making themselves useful. Behavior is organized around giving, sometimes at the cost of their own limits.
bullets: Generous and helpful — moving toward people, anticipating needs, offering before being asked.
Adept at adjusting to others — becoming what the relationship seems to call for.
Boundaries can be soft; saying no is hard when being needed is how you feel secure.
Over-giving can lead to depletion and a quiet resentment when it isn't reciprocated.
You may step in to help even when help wasn't wanted — the giving has its own momentum.
Real generosity is a gift; the work is giving freely rather than to secure love in return.
behaving.inquiry: Where are you giving in order to be needed rather than because it's freely chosen?

inquiry_lines: When you stop tracking what others need, what do you notice you need?
What feelings do you tend to hide because they feel too needy to show?
Where are you giving in order to be needed rather than because it's freely chosen?

wing_a.body:
The One wing brings principle, structure, and standards into the Two. Where the core Two focuses on relationship and warmth, the One wing adds conscientiousness and a sense of what's right. Twos with a One wing tend to be more dutiful, serious, and self-controlled in how they help.

At their best: warm and principled — generous care guided by integrity.

wing_b.body:
The Three wing brings ambition, image-awareness, and drive into the Two. Where the core Two helps quietly, the Three wing adds visibility and accomplishment — helping in ways that are seen and valued. Twos with a Three wing tend to be more outgoing, competent, and socially adept.

At their best: warm and effective — care that gets things done and brings people along.

stress.narrative: Under significant pressure, Twos can shift toward Eight energy — becoming more demanding, forceful, and confrontational. The warmth gives way to a harder edge, often when the giving has gone unreturned for too long. Noticed early, it's a signal that real needs have been suppressed past their limit.
stress.resource_card: Under pressure: demanding, forceful, confrontational. Consciously accessed: directness, healthy assertion, the ability to name your own needs.

security.narrative: When Twos feel genuinely safe and supported, they move toward Four energy — turning attention inward, getting in touch with their own feelings and needs, and expressing their authentic self rather than shaping it to others.
security.resource_card: In flow: inwardness, authenticity, contact with your own feelings. Available now: tending to your own emotional life as fully as you tend to others'.

strengths.title: Genuine Warmth
strengths.body: A natural ability to make others feel seen, cared for, and valued — generous attention that lands as real love.

strengths.title: Emotional Attunement
strengths.body: A gift for sensing what others feel and need, often before they say it — making you a deeply supportive presence.

strengths.title: Devoted Generosity
strengths.body: A willingness to show up for people fully — the friend, partner, or colleague who reliably gives of themselves.

challenges.title: Self-Neglect
challenges.body: Your own needs fade behind everyone else's — so consistently that you may lose track of what you actually want.

challenges.title: Pride and Indirectness
challenges.body: Difficulty admitting need or asking directly — the helper role can make receiving feel unsafe.

challenges.title: Conditional Giving
challenges.body: Generosity that quietly expects love in return — and the resentment that builds when it isn't reciprocated.

practices.intro: These practices can help you build on what's already working and work with the patterns that can hold you back.
bullets: Practice naming your own needs out loud. “I need…” is not weakness — it's the honesty that lets others actually love you.
Notice the ledger. When you feel resentful, look for the giving that quietly expected something back.
Let yourself receive without immediately repaying. Accepting help is its own practice — and it's how relationships balance.
Pause before helping. Ask whether help was wanted, and whether you're giving freely or to secure connection.
Tend to your inner life. Moving toward your security point (Type 4) means making your own feelings as real as everyone else's.

communication.subhead: Communication Style — Warm, Attuned, and Relationship-First
bullets: You communicate with warmth and personal attention — people feel cared for in conversation with you.
You read emotional subtext quickly and respond to what others feel, not just what they say.
You tend to lead with the relationship, sometimes softening your own message to protect it.
Your own needs and opinions can stay unspoken, tucked behind your attention to the other person.
watch_for: Others may not know what you actually want, because you've prioritized their comfort over your clarity.
Hinting at needs rather than stating them puts the burden on others to guess — and they often don't.
Naming what you need directly is a gift to the relationship, not a threat to it.
Letting your real opinion show — even when it might disappoint — builds trust deeper than constant agreement.

conflict.subhead: Conflict Style — Toward the Person — Smoothing and Connecting
bullets: Conflict threatens connection, so the instinct is to repair, soothe, and restore the relationship quickly.
You may give more, accommodate, or take on blame to keep the bond intact.
Direct anger is uncomfortable to express — it can come out as hurt or as a sudden harder edge instead.
When giving goes unreturned long enough, resentment can break through with surprising force.
working_with: Smoothing things over can leave your real grievance unspoken — and it tends to resurface later.
The hurt underneath the helping is worth naming directly, before it builds into resentment.
You're allowed to have needs in a conflict, not just to tend to the other person's.
The question worth sitting with: am I keeping this relationship, or keeping myself out of it?

center.subhead: Coming Back to Center — Coming Home to Yourself
bullets: As a Heart Center type, you process the world through relationship and emotional connection.
The Heart Center's organizing emotion is shame, and for Twos it surfaces as the fear of being unwanted unless useful.
Presence, for you, means turning some of that exquisite attention back toward yourself.
The goal isn't to give less; it's to include yourself among the people you care for.
off_center: Signals: depletion, resentment, losing track of your own needs, helping that has a compulsive edge.
The return path: ask “what do I need right now?” and let the answer matter as much as anyone else's.
Notice the moment you reshape yourself to fit a relationship — that's the pattern, gently visible.
Moving toward your security point (Type 4) means tending your own emotional life as fully as others'.

comparison.core_motivation: To be loved and needed — earning connection by giving and meeting others' needs.
comparison.focus: Other people's needs, feelings, and moods; the state of important relationships.
comparison.energy: Helping, attuning, anticipating needs, moving toward people, making oneself indispensable.
comparison.gifts: Warm, generous, attuned, supportive, relationally gifted, deeply caring.
comparison.challenges: Self-neglecting, indirect about needs, prideful about receiving, prone to conditional giving.

subtype_sp2.name: Self-Preservation Two
subtype_sp2.tagline: The Family Nurturer — warmth with a childlike, reciprocal undercurrent (countertype)
subtype_sp2.narrative:
Self-Preservation Twos build warm, personable relationships and take care of others so they will be taken care of in return. There’s a childlike, endearing quality, and often an unspoken entitlement — “I’ve given so much, now it’s my turn“ — or its inverse, false modesty. The giving has a reciprocal undercurrent: care offered with an expectation of care received.

This is the countertype of Type 2. SP Twos can look more childlike, dependent, or even needy than the classic giving Two, and the helping can carry a conditional quality that isn’t obvious on the surface. The pride that resists receiving in other Twos is softer here — there’s a more direct, if unspoken, hope to be looked after.

thinking: Attention goes to close relationships and to being cared for in return.
Runs a silent reciprocation ledger; what’s been given, and what’s owed back.
More focused on a small circle of important others.
feeling: Warmth comes with a childlike, endearing quality that draws others in.
A quiet entitlement (“now it’s my turn”) or its inverse (false modesty) is always present.
Hurt surfaces when the reciprocity doesn’t come, though it’s rarely named directly.
behaving: Builds personable bonds and shows care to those close to them.
Can appear more needy than the classic self-sufficient Two.
The helping carries conditions — care given with care expected in return.

shifts: The giving turns toward security and a close circle — care offered partly to ensure care received.
You may look more childlike and endearing than the classic Two, with needs closer to the surface.
The growing edge is the ledger — noticing the reciprocity the giving quietly expects.

subtype_so2.name: Social Two
subtype_so2.tagline: The Ambassador — warmth aimed at the group, influence, and visible standing
subtype_so2.narrative:
Social Twos build self-esteem through social approval and visible contribution, becoming indispensable within organizations, groups, and causes. They are often more comfortable just left of center stage — the trusted right hand, the connector everyone relies on. The helping is aimed at the collective, and standing within the group matters.

The ambition here can look like Type Three achievement-orientation. SO Twos can be highly visible, accomplished people whose underlying Two motivation — connection and worth through being essential to the group — is masked by their professional success. The question is always whether the drive is for the achievement itself or for being indispensable to the people in it.

thinking: Attention goes to the group — who matters, where influence sits, how to become essential to it.
Reads social standing carefully: knowing the right people and holding a valued place.
Strategic about contribution, with an eye on how the giving is received by the collective.
feeling: Self-worth rises and falls with social approval and the sense of being indispensable.
Pride takes the form of being the one the group can't do without.
Personal needs get subordinated to maintaining standing and connection in the group.
behaving: Becomes indispensable within organizations and causes — the trusted, connecting presence.
Helps visibly and ambitiously, often from just left of center stage.
Can look like a high-achieving Three, with the Two motivation underneath.

shifts: The giving aims at the group — becoming essential to the collective rather than to one person.
You may look ambitious and accomplished, with the Two motivation masked by visible success.
The growing edge is asking whether the drive is for the achievement, or for being needed by the people in it.

subtype_sx2.name: One-to-One Two
subtype_sx2.tagline: The Healer — warmth concentrated into magnetic, intense connection
subtype_sx2.narrative:
One-to-One Twos channel all their interpersonal attunement into winning the approval and devotion of selected significant others. There’s a magnetic, sometimes seductive quality to the energy — not necessarily sexual, but charged with the desire to be irresistible to the people who matter. The giving is intense and personal, aimed at becoming indispensable to one or a few.

The aggressive side of this subtype can surprise — this is a Two who will demand recognition and connection rather than quietly earn it. They can appear charming and magnetic but also intense and insistent. The need underneath is for a chosen person to find them essential, even irresistible.

thinking: Attention concentrates on significant others, winning their approval, devotion.
Reads what would make them irresistible to a chosen person, and puts energy towards that.
Less focused on the group; the energy goes toward intense individual bonds.
feeling: A magnetic, charged quality runs through the connection driven by a need to be indispensable or irresistible.
Need and intensity are closer to the surface, often expressed as demanding.
Rejection by a chosen person lands hard, threatening their sense of being essential.
behaving: Pours attunement into selected significant others, becoming indispensable.
Can be charming and seductive but also insistent, even aggressive, in claiming connection.
Helps intensely and personally, aimed at one or a few rather than the many.

shifts: The giving concentrates into intense, magnetic bonds — being irresistible to chosen people.
You may look more demanding or seductive than the classic quiet helper — need is closer to the surface.
The growing edge is the insistence on connection: noticing where the giving becomes a claim.

type_3.name: The Performer

description.worldview: Threes experience the world as a place that rewards success and admires winners. Being effective, accomplished, and impressive is how you earn love and value — and the fear underneath is that without achievement, you'd be worth nothing.
description.core_motivation: To be successful, admired, and seen as a winner — earning worth and love through accomplishment, effectiveness, and a polished image.

thinking.intro: For Threes, attention goes to goals, tasks, and how things are being received. The mind is efficient and outcome-focused, quick to read what success looks like in a given context and how to deliver it.
bullets: Attention goes to goals and outcomes — what needs to get done and how to do it efficiently.
Thinking reads the room for what success looks like here, then adapts to deliver it.
Feelings can get set aside in favor of the task; emotions are a delay, not a guide.
The mind tracks how you're being perceived — image is a constant background calculation.
Multitasking and momentum come naturally; slowing down can feel like falling behind.
The line between the real self and the successful image can blur, even to you.
thinking.inquiry: Who are you when there's no goal to achieve and no one watching?

feeling.intro: Threes often run ahead of their feelings — staying in motion partly because stopping lets emotions catch up. The image is managed so smoothly that the person inside it can be hard to find.
bullets: Feelings get deferred in service of the goal — emotions are managed, postponed, or worked around.
The emotional life is real but under-attended; productivity can be a way of staying ahead of it.
Self-worth is tied tightly to performance — success feels like love, failure like worthlessness.
There's often a quiet fear that the real self, beneath the achievements, isn't enough.
Vulnerability is risky; showing struggle threatens the competent image.
Slowing down enough to feel is both the hardest thing and the doorway to authenticity.
feeling.inquiry: What feelings catch up with you when you finally stop moving?

behaving.intro: Threes tend to be energetic, efficient, and high-performing. Behavior is organized around getting results and being seen to succeed — adapting smoothly to whatever the context rewards.
bullets: Driven and efficient — you set goals, build momentum, and deliver results others rely on.
Adapts the image to context — becoming whatever version of successful the situation values.
Stays in motion; rest and downtime can feel uncomfortable or even unsafe.
Image management runs underneath — presenting the polished, winning version of yourself.
Can overwork and burn out, mistaking constant doing for genuine worth.
Real competence is a gift; the work is letting the results come from the true self, not the performed one.
behaving.inquiry: Where are you performing success instead of living it?

inquiry_lines: Who are you when there's no goal to achieve and no one watching?
What feelings catch up with you when you finally stop moving?
Where are you performing success instead of living it?

wing_a.body:
The Two wing brings warmth, charm, and relational focus into the Three. Where the core Three drives toward results, the Two wing adds interpersonal warmth and a desire to be liked. Threes with a Two wing tend to be more people-oriented, charming, and emotionally engaging.

At their best: effective and warm — success that brings people along and lifts them up.

wing_b.body:
The Four wing brings depth, sensitivity, and a desire for authenticity into the Three. Where the core Three polishes the image, the Four wing adds introspection and creative individuality. Threes with a Four wing tend to be more emotionally complex, artistic, and concerned with being genuine.

At their best: effective and authentic — accomplishment with real depth and originality.

stress.narrative: Under significant pressure, Threes can shift toward Nine energy — becoming disengaged, diffuse, and unable to mobilize. The usual drive stalls out into procrastination, distraction, and a checked-out numbness. Noticed early, it's a signal that the engine has been running too hard for too long.
stress.resource_card: Under pressure: disengagement, procrastination, numbness. Consciously accessed: ease, presence, the ability to rest without performing.

security.narrative: When Threes feel genuinely safe and supported, they move toward Six energy — becoming more loyal, collaborative, and committed to others rather than only to outcomes. The focus shifts from personal success to shared purpose and genuine connection with a team.
security.resource_card: In flow: loyalty, collaboration, commitment to others. Available now: investing in shared purpose, not just personal achievement.

strengths.title: Drive and Effectiveness
strengths.body: A powerful ability to set goals and achieve them — getting things done and inspiring others to perform at their best.

strengths.title: Adaptability
strengths.body: A talent for reading what a situation needs and rising to it — versatile, capable, and quick to deliver.

strengths.title: Motivating Presence
strengths.body: A natural role-model energy that lifts the people around you — competence others want to follow.

challenges.title: Identity Through Performance
challenges.body: Worth fused with achievement — so that failure feels like worthlessness and the real self gets lost behind the image.

challenges.title: Deferred Feeling
challenges.body: Emotions postponed in service of goals — staying so busy that the inner life goes unattended.

challenges.title: Image Over Authenticity
challenges.body: Adapting the self to what each context rewards — until it's hard to know who you are beneath the performance.

practices.intro: These practices can help you build on what's already working and work with the patterns that can hold you back.
bullets: Practice stopping on purpose. Stillness lets the feelings catch up — and reconnecting with them is how you find the self beneath the image.
Separate worth from results. You are not your last achievement; notice when failure feels like annihilation rather than information.
Tell someone the unpolished truth. Letting a trusted person see the struggle, not just the success, is where real connection lives.
Ask what you actually want, not what would impress. The goal worth pursuing is the one that's yours, not the context's.
Invest in people for their own sake. Moving toward your security point (Type 6) means loyalty and shared purpose over solo wins.

communication.subhead: Communication Style — Polished, Efficient, and Goal-Oriented
bullets: You communicate clearly and efficiently — focused on outcomes, next steps, and getting to the point.
You read your audience and adapt your message to land well with them.
You project competence and confidence, presenting the capable version of yourself.
Feelings and process can get skipped in favor of results and momentum.
watch_for: Efficiency can read as impatience — others may feel processed rather than met.
The polished presentation can create distance; people sense the image and miss the person.
Letting some unpolished truth through — a doubt, a struggle — builds the trust that performance can't.
Slowing down to connect, not just to deliver, makes your competence land as leadership rather than pressure.

conflict.subhead: Conflict Style — Solve and Move On — Staying Effective
bullets: Conflict gets treated as a problem to solve efficiently so everyone can get back to productivity.
You stay composed and competent, managing the situation rather than dwelling in the emotion of it.
You'd rather fix the issue and move forward than sit in unresolved feeling.
The emotional layer can get bypassed — solved on the surface while the feeling underneath persists.
working_with: Solving the problem isn't the same as resolving the relationship — the feeling part still needs tending.
Bypassing emotion to stay effective can leave others feeling unheard even when the issue is 'fixed.'
Staying present to the discomfort, rather than managing past it, deepens trust.
The question worth sitting with: am I resolving this, or just getting the win and moving on?

center.subhead: Coming Back to Center — Finding the Self Beneath the Image
bullets: As a Heart Center type, you process the world through relationship and how you're being received.
The Heart Center's organizing emotion is shame, and for Threes it drives the fear that the unaccomplished self isn't enough.
Presence, for you, means letting the doing stop long enough to feel who's underneath.
The goal isn't to achieve less; it's to know the self that exists whether or not it succeeds.
off_center: Signals: relentless busyness, image-management, a creeping sense that you're performing rather than living.
The return path: stop and feel. The emotions you've outrun carry the information about who you actually are.
Notice when you're adapting the self to win approval — that's the pattern, gently visible.
