Moving toward your security point (Type 6) means valuing loyalty and connection over the next win.

comparison.core_motivation: To be successful, admired, and seen as a winner — worth earned through accomplishment.
comparison.focus: Goals, tasks, results, and how one is being perceived and received.
comparison.energy: Achieving, adapting, building momentum, managing image, staying in productive motion.
comparison.gifts: Driven, effective, adaptable, motivating, competent, results-oriented.
comparison.challenges: Identity fused with performance, deferred feeling, image over authenticity, overwork.

subtype_sp3.name: Self-Preservation Three
subtype_sp3.tagline: The Diligent Worker — success through hard work and material security (countertype)
subtype_sp3.narrative:
Self-Preservation Threes channel their drive into material success, financial security, and the tangible markers of a well-run life. They prefer to be seen as hardworking and reliable rather than flashy or self-promoting — the image being managed is, paradoxically, the image of someone who doesn’t manage image. Quality, productivity, and doing things properly matter here.

This is the countertype of Type 3, and it can look surprisingly like a One because of the emphasis on doing things correctly rather than showing off. The classic ambitious, image-conscious Three doesn’t fit cleanly. They presented an image of humility and often have genuinely complicated feelings about being recognized for their accomplishments.

thinking: Attention goes to security, productivity, and the tangible markers of a well-run life.
Focused on doing things properly and efficiently rather than on visible self-promotion.
Tracks competence and reliability more than applause.
feeling: Self-worth is tied to being hardworking and capable, not to being admired publicly.
Has complicated feelings about recognition — wants it, but finds overt display uncomfortable.
The fear of failure shows up as anxiety about security rather than about status.
behaving: Works hard and steadily, presenting as modest and reliable rather than flashy.
Builds material security and tangible accomplishment as the proof of worth.
Downplays the image work itself, which can look like One-ish conscientiousness.

shifts: The drive turns toward security and quality — success measured in reliability rather than applause.
You may be mistaken for a One: hardworking, proper, uncomfortable with overt self-promotion.
The growing edge is the complicated relationship to recognition — wanting it while finding display uneasy.

subtype_so3.name: Social Three
subtype_so3.tagline: The Politician — success through status, influence, and visible standing
subtype_so3.narrative:
Social Threes direct the success drive toward visible status — knowing the right people, holding influential roles, being effective and admired within groups and institutions. They are natural political operators with high social intelligence, attuned to how they're being received and skilled at being received well.

This is the most visible Three pattern, and it's easy to read as genuine leadership rather than image management — the social skill is real. But the underlying question is always how they're being perceived, and their relationship to disapproval or failure in social contexts reveals the structure underneath the polish.

thinking: Attention goes to status and standing — the right roles, the right people, visible influence.
Reads social dynamics with high intelligence and positions accordingly.
Tracks how they're being received as a near-constant background calculation.
feeling: Self-worth rises and falls with social recognition and visible success.
Approval feels like love; disapproval in a group lands as a real threat.
The polished social confidence can sit on top of a fear of not measuring up.
behaving: Cultivates visible status and influence — effective, admired, well-connected.
Adapts the image expertly to whatever the group values most.
Operates politically with genuine skill, which reads as leadership.

shifts: The drive turns toward status and standing — success measured in influence and recognition.
You may read as a natural leader, the social skill masking the image-management underneath.
The growing edge is the relationship to disapproval — what happens when the group doesn't respond as expected.

subtype_sx3.name: One-to-One Three
subtype_sx3.tagline: The Star — success through charisma and personal magnetism
subtype_sx3.narrative:
One-to-One Threes focus the performance energy on charisma and personal magnetism — being the one whose presence fills a room, who's attractive and compelling to specific people. Personal impact matters more than institutional prestige here; the goal is to be the best for, and most desired by, the people who matter.

SX Threes can look like Twos because of the emphasis on creating connection and winning personal attention. The focus on charming specific others, rather than achieving institutional success, can obscure the achievement motivation. The tell is whether the interpersonal skill serves the other's needs (Two) or serves their own impact and desirability (Three).

thinking: Attention goes to personal magnetism — being attractive, compelling, and impactful to specific people.
Reads what would make them desirable to the person who matters, and becomes it.
Focused on individual impact more than institutional standing.
feeling: Self-worth is tied to being found magnetic and desirable by significant others.
Charisma is the currency; being wanted feels like succeeding.
Underneath the magnetism is the fear that the unperformed self wouldn't be enough.
behaving: Cultivates charisma and personal magnetism — the presence that fills a room.
Adapts the self to be the most compelling version for specific people.
Can look like a Two in the focus on connection — but the aim is impact, not service.

shifts: The drive concentrates into charisma and magnetism — being desired by the people who matter.
You may be mistaken for a Two: focused on connection, winning personal attention.
The growing edge is whether the interpersonal skill serves the other, or serves your own desirability.

type_4.name: The Individualist

description.worldview: Fours experience the world as a place where something essential is missing — a sense that others have a wholeness or belonging they themselves lack. Seeking depth, authenticity, and meaning is how you reach for the connection and significance that feel just out of reach.
description.core_motivation: To be authentic, deeply understood, and significant — finding meaning and identity by embracing the full depth of their feelings and the longing for what's missing.

thinking.intro: For Fours, attention goes to what's missing and to the gap between the ideal and the ordinary. The mind is drawn to depth, meaning, and the ways the present moment falls short of what could be.
bullets: Attention goes to what's absent — what's missing here, what others have that you don't.
Thinking is comparative: measuring the self against others and the present against an ideal.
The mind is drawn toward depth and meaning, away from the surface and the mundane.
Longing has a pull of its own — the distant and unavailable can feel more vivid than what's present.
Identity is a recurring question: who am I, really, and what makes me different?
There's a sensitivity to beauty and significance that ordinary life rarely satisfies.
thinking.inquiry: What feels missing right now — and what would having it actually change?

feeling.intro: Fours live most fully in feeling — emotions run deep, wide, and vivid, and there's a willingness to stay with the difficult ones others avoid. The risk is identifying so closely with the feeling that it becomes the self.
bullets: Feelings are deep, vivid, and central — emotional intensity is where life feels most real.
There's a comfort with melancholy and longing that others find hard to stay with.
Moods can pull strongly, coloring everything until they shift.
Identity can fuse with feeling — “I am my sadness” rather than “I feel sad right now.”
Envy of others' apparent wholeness can run underneath, quiet but persistent.
The capacity to feel fully is a gift — the work is feeling without drowning in it.
feeling.inquiry: Which feelings do you hold onto, and what would it mean to let them move through?

behaving.intro: Fours tend to be expressive, individualistic, and emotionally honest. Behavior is shaped by the search for authenticity — being true to inner experience, even when it sets them apart.
bullets: Expressive and authentic — bringing real feeling and individuality into how you show up.
Drawn to create and express — turning inner experience into something meaningful or beautiful.
Can withdraw to protect the inner world, especially when it feels misunderstood.
The pull toward the unavailable can shape choices — wanting what's distant, cooling toward what's near.
Self-expression sometimes tips into dramatizing, amplifying feeling to feel real.
Emotional honesty is a gift to others — permission to be real that few people offer.
behaving.inquiry: Where does the pull toward what's distant keep you from what's already here?

inquiry_lines: What feels missing right now — and what would having it actually change?
Which feelings do you hold onto, and what would it mean to let them move through?
Where does the pull toward what's distant keep you from what's already here?

wing_a.body:
The Three wing brings drive, ambition, and image-awareness into the Four. Where the core Four turns inward, the Three wing adds outward momentum and a desire to be seen and accomplished. Fours with a Three wing tend to be more productive, expressive in public, and oriented toward making their mark.

At their best: authentic and accomplished — depth that gets expressed and recognized.

wing_b.body:
The Five wing brings withdrawal, depth, and intellectual focus into the Four. Where the core Four feels intensely, the Five wing adds analysis and a need for solitude. Fours with a Five wing tend to be more private, cerebral, and unconventional, channeling feeling into ideas and creative work.

At their best: authentic and insightful — feeling deepened by understanding.

stress.narrative: Under significant pressure, Fours can shift toward Two energy — becoming more focused on others, over-giving, and seeking connection by being needed. The inward focus turns outward, sometimes losing the self in attending to someone else. Noticed early, it's a signal that the longing has gone looking for relief in the wrong place.
stress.resource_card: Under pressure: over-giving, clinging, losing self in others. Consciously accessed: generosity, warmth, and genuine care for others' needs.

security.narrative: When Fours feel genuinely safe and supported, they move toward One energy — becoming more disciplined, structured, and able to act on their ideals rather than only feel them. Emotion gets channeled into focused, principled action and follow-through.
security.resource_card: In flow: discipline, structure, principled action. Available now: turning feeling and vision into steady, grounded follow-through.

strengths.title: Emotional Depth
strengths.body: A capacity to feel and stay with the full range of human emotion — including the hard feelings others avoid.

strengths.title: Authenticity
strengths.body: A commitment to being real rather than conventional — and an ability to give others permission to be real too.

strengths.title: Creative Sensitivity
strengths.body: An eye for beauty, meaning, and significance — turning inner experience into expression that moves people.

challenges.title: Comparison and Envy
challenges.body: A habit of measuring against others and finding the self lacking — focusing on what's missing rather than what's here.

challenges.title: Mood Identification
challenges.body: Fusing identity with feeling — so that a passing emotion becomes a fixed sense of who you are.

challenges.title: Longing for the Absent
challenges.body: A pull toward the distant and unavailable that can devalue what's actually present and available.

practices.intro: These practices can help you build on what's already working and work with the patterns that can hold you back.
bullets: Notice feelings as weather, not identity. “I feel sad” is true; “I am sad” fuses you to a passing state. The distinction creates room to move.
Practice appreciating what's present. The pull toward the absent is strong — deliberately turning toward what's already here rebalances it.
Catch the comparison in real time. The measuring against others is automatic; seeing it lets you set it down.
Take ordinary action even without inspiration. Moving toward your security point (Type 1) means structure and follow-through, not waiting for the feeling.
Let yourself be understood as you are, not only in your depths. Connection doesn't require the full intensity every time.

communication.subhead: Communication Style — Expressive, Personal, and Emotionally Honest
bullets: You communicate with feeling and authenticity — bringing real emotion and personal truth into the conversation.
You're drawn to depth and meaning, away from small talk and surface.
You express individuality, sometimes setting yourself apart on purpose.
You may withdraw when you feel misunderstood, going quiet rather than bridging the gap.
watch_for: Intensity can overwhelm — not everyone is ready to go as deep as quickly as you are.
Withdrawing when hurt leaves others guessing; naming the disconnection is more bridging than retreating.
Not every exchange needs full emotional depth — the surface has its place too.
Letting yourself be understood plainly, not only in your complexity, makes connection easier for both sides.

conflict.subhead: Conflict Style — Into the Feeling — Intensity
bullets: Conflict gets felt deeply and personally — the emotional stakes register fully and immediately.
You move toward the feeling rather than away, willing to stay in difficult emotional territory.
Withdrawal is one response; intense expression is another, depending on the moment.
The hurt can be amplified by comparison — a sense of being uniquely misunderstood or wronged.
working_with: The depth of your feeling is real, and it can also magnify the conflict beyond its actual size.
Withdrawing to protect yourself can read as punishment; staying connected serves the repair.
Not every conflict is about your significance or difference — some are just ordinary friction.
The question worth sitting with: am I in this feeling, or have I become it?

center.subhead: Coming Back to Center — Coming Back to What's Here
bullets: As a Heart Center type, you process the world through emotion and the question of identity.
The Heart Center's organizing emotion is shame, and for Fours it surfaces as a felt sense of being flawed or missing something essential.
Presence, for you, means feeling fully without becoming the feeling — and turning toward the present.
The goal isn't to feel less; it's to stay grounded in what's actually here while you feel.
off_center: Signals: comparison, longing for the absent, melancholy that pulls you out of the present moment.
The return path: turn toward what's here. Concrete appreciation of the present rebalances the pull toward the missing.
Notice when a passing mood is hardening into an identity — that's the pattern, gently visible.
Moving toward your security point (Type 1) means grounding feeling in structure and steady action.

comparison.core_motivation: To be authentic, deeply understood, and significant — embracing the full depth of feeling.
comparison.focus: What's missing, the ideal versus the ordinary, identity, depth and meaning.
comparison.energy: Feeling deeply, expressing authentically, creating, longing for the absent, seeking significance.
comparison.gifts: Emotionally deep, authentic, creative, sensitive, attuned to beauty and meaning.
comparison.challenges: Prone to comparison and envy, identifies with mood, longs for the absent over the present.

subtype_sp4.name: Self-Preservation Four
subtype_sp4.tagline: The Creative Individualist — suffering met with dauntless endurance (countertype)
subtype_sp4.narrative:
Self-Preservation Fours throw themselves into life with a dauntless, sometimes reckless energy — jumping into new situations, taking risks, or pursuing unorthodox paths when the standard options feel inauthentic. Rather than displaying their suffering, they internalize it and work hard not to be defeated by the sense of not being enough.

This is the countertype of Type 4, and it often doesn’t wear the melancholic, inward, longing quality classically associated with the type. SP Fours can look driven and resilient — almost like a Three — refusing to be beaten by the feeling of deficiency. The suffering is internalized rather than expressed, which is exactly what makes this Four hard to recognize.

thinking: Attention goes to enduring and overcoming, proving they can push through their suffering.
The comparison and sense of lack are present but channeled into doing.
Drawn to the unconventional and authentic, sometimes through risk and reinvention.
feeling: Suffering is internalized rather than shown, bearing it privately, presenting a resilient front.
The longing and deficiency are real but rarely revealed to others.
Underneath this is the same Four longing, but energy goes to masking it.
behaving: Throws caution to the wind — jumping into new situations and taking risks.
Works tenaciously, refusing to be defeated by their sense of lack.
Can look driven and resilient, even Three-like, rather than forlorn.

shifts: The Four longing is met with endurance — internalized and channeled into drive rather than displayed.
You may be mistaken for a Three or a Seven: resilient, active, refusing to be defeated.
The growing edge is the suffering underneath the tenacity — what you're proving, and to whom.

subtype_so4.name: Social Four
subtype_so4.tagline: The Critical Commentator — deficiency felt through social comparison and shame
subtype_so4.narrative:
Social Fours feel their deficiency most acutely in social contexts, through comparison to others' status, belonging, or abilities. They often seek honorable roles — the emotional truth-teller, the one who names what's missing or wrong in the group. The shame is more acute for this subtype than the others, and it shapes a particular sensitivity to where they stand.

The social orientation can look like engaged social criticism rather than personal melancholy. SO Fours can become the voice that speaks the uncomfortable truth into a group, and this role can hide the underlying shame and sense of not-belonging. The relationship between their critique and their own longing to belong is the heart of the pattern.

thinking: Attention goes to social comparison — where they stand, who belongs, what they lack relative to others.
Drawn to naming what's missing or wrong, often in the role of social critic or truth-teller.
Tracks belonging and status with a sensitivity sharpened by shame.
feeling: Shame is more acute here than in the other Four subtypes — felt keenly in social comparison.
Longing focuses on belonging and being honored within the group.
The melancholy can hide behind the role of the one who names what's wrong.
behaving: Takes on honorable or truth-telling roles — speaking what's missing into the group.
Engages in social criticism that can mask personal melancholy.
Positions self in relation to the group, often as both insider and outsider.

shifts: The deficiency is felt socially — through comparison and the question of where you belong.
You may look like an engaged social critic rather than a melancholic Four — the shame hides in the role.
The growing edge is the link between your critique and your own longing to belong and be honored.

subtype_sx4.name: One-to-One Four
subtype_sx4.tagline: The Dramatic Person — longing charged with competition and intensity
subtype_sx4.narrative:
One-to-One Fours are motivated by competition and intensity. Another's talent or fortune becomes a personal challenge, and their own sense of value rises and falls in comparison. They seek intensity of connection — with partners, with creative work, with experience itself — and can be demanding, even combative, in pursuit of it.

The competitive, sometimes aggressive edge of SX Fours doesn't fit the quiet, moody, inward image of the type. They can look intense, striving, even confrontational — more like an Eight or a Three than the classic Four. The envy here turns active: rather than withdrawing in longing, they compete to claim what they feel is rightfully theirs.

thinking: Attention goes to comparison as competition — another's gift becomes a personal challenge to meet or beat.
Drawn to intensity in connection and experience; the ordinary feels like not enough.
Value rises and falls against rivals, fueling a striving, sometimes combative focus.
feeling: Envy turns active and competitive — felt as a charge to prove and claim, not just to long for.
Emotional intensity runs high, expressed more openly and forcefully than in other Fours.
Underneath the competition is the familiar Four ache for significance and authentic connection.
behaving: Competes — for attention, for recognition, for the intensity of being chosen.
Can be demanding, striving, even confrontational in pursuit of connection and value.
Channels longing into intense creative or relational pursuit rather than quiet withdrawal.

shifts: The longing turns competitive — another's gift becomes a personal challenge to rise to.
You may be mistaken for an Eight or a Three: intense, striving, confrontational rather than withdrawn.
The growing edge is the active envy — noticing where comparison becomes a charge to prove and claim.

type_5.name: The Observer

description.worldview: Fives experience the world as intrusive and depleting — a place that demands more than they have to give. Conserving energy, gathering knowledge, and maintaining privacy is how you stay self-sufficient and protected against being overwhelmed or found wanting.
description.core_motivation: To be capable, self-sufficient, and unintruded upon — protecting limited inner resources by gathering knowledge and keeping a careful distance from demand.

thinking.intro: For Fives, attention goes to understanding — observing, analyzing, and gathering knowledge from a step back. The mind is the primary tool, and detachment from feeling makes it sharper.
bullets: Attention goes to understanding — observing and analyzing rather than participating.
Thinking happens at a remove; stepping back to study is safer than stepping in.
Knowledge feels like competence and security — knowing enough is a form of preparedness.
Emotions get detached from in the moment, to be processed later in private.
The mind compartmentalizes — keeping different areas of life, and people, in separate boxes.
There's a pull toward expertise and depth in chosen areas, away from broad social demand.
thinking.inquiry: What do you understand thoroughly that you've never actually lived?

feeling.intro: Fives tend to detach from feeling in the moment, experiencing emotions more fully in solitude after the fact. The inner life is real but guarded, kept separate from the demands of the outer world.
bullets: Feelings get detached from in real time, then felt later in the safety of solitude.
Emotional expression can feel depleting and exposing — easier to think than to feel out loud.
The inner world is rich but private, shared with very few.
There's a fear that needs and feelings, if let out, would overwhelm or deplete you.
Warmth is real but reserved — given to a chosen few rather than broadcast.
Reconnecting with feeling in the moment, not just afterward, is the growing edge.
feeling.inquiry: What happens to your feelings when you're with people versus alone?

behaving.intro: Fives tend to be private, self-contained, and economical with their energy. Behavior is organized around conserving resources — limiting demands, maintaining independence, and retreating to replenish.
bullets: Private and self-contained — guarding time, energy, and personal space carefully.
Minimizes needs and dependence; self-sufficiency feels safer than relying on others.
Withdraws to replenish — solitude is necessary, not optional.
Can detach from people and demands to protect a limited store of energy.
Engages deeply in chosen areas of interest while staying remote from much else.
The capacity for focused, independent depth is a real gift — the work is staying connected too.
behaving.inquiry: Where do you withdraw to conserve energy that connection might actually restore?

inquiry_lines: What do you understand thoroughly that you've never actually lived?
What happens to your feelings when you're with people versus alone?
Where do you withdraw to conserve energy that connection might actually restore?

wing_a.body:
The Four wing brings emotional depth, creativity, and individuality into the Five. Where the core Five analyzes, the Four wing adds feeling and aesthetic sensibility. Fives with a Four wing tend to be more expressive, original, and drawn to meaning as well as knowledge.

At their best: insightful and expressive — understanding infused with feeling.

wing_b.body:
The Six wing brings loyalty, caution, and a focus on security into the Five. Where the core Five gathers knowledge for its own sake, the Six wing adds practical vigilance and commitment to people and systems. Fives with a Six wing tend to be more grounded, collaborative, and oriented toward trust.

At their best: insightful and steady — understanding put in service of what matters.

stress.narrative: Under significant pressure, Fives can shift toward Seven energy — becoming scattered, restless, and prone to mental escape into multiple ideas and possibilities. The careful focus fragments into distraction. Noticed early, it's a signal that the demands have outpaced the available resources.
stress.resource_card: Under pressure: scattered, restless, escaping into possibility. Consciously accessed: spontaneity, breadth, and engagement with life's options.

security.narrative: When Fives feel genuinely safe and resourced, they move toward Eight energy — becoming more assertive, embodied, and willing to take direct action in the world. The detachment gives way to presence; thinking translates into decisive engagement.
security.resource_card: In flow: assertion, embodiment, decisive action. Available now: bringing your understanding into the world through direct engagement.

strengths.title: Depth of Understanding
strengths.body: A powerful capacity to observe, analyze, and master complex subjects — clear thinking others rely on for perspective.

strengths.title: Self-Sufficiency
strengths.body: An ability to stand on your own, think independently, and stay calm and objective when others are reactive.

strengths.title: Perceptive Insight
strengths.body: A gift for seeing patterns and truths beneath the surface — the quiet observer who notices what others miss.

challenges.title: Detachment
challenges.body: Withdrawing from feeling and from people — so consistently that connection and presence can atrophy.

challenges.title: Hoarding Resources
challenges.body: Guarding energy, time, and self so tightly that you give and receive less than relationships need.

challenges.title: Living in the Mind
challenges.body: Substituting understanding for experience — knowing about life from a step back rather than being in it.

practices.intro: These practices can help you build on what's already working and work with the patterns that can hold you back.
bullets: Practice feeling in real time, not just in review. Naming an emotion as it happens — even silently — reconnects the head and the heart.
Notice the reflex to withdraw and conserve. Some demands deplete; some connections restore. Test which is which rather than assuming.
Experiment with engaging before you feel fully prepared. Living the thing teaches what observing it never will.
Let trusted people in further than feels comfortable. Sharing the inner world builds the relationships that make demand feel less threatening.
Bring understanding into action. Moving toward your security point (Type 8) means embodying what you know, not just holding it.

communication.subhead: Communication Style — Precise, Reserved, and Considered
bullets: You communicate thoughtfully and precisely — measured, well-reasoned, economical with words.
You prefer to think before speaking, and may go quiet to process rather than react.
You share selectively, keeping much of the inner world private.
You're more comfortable with ideas and depth than with emotional or social small talk.
watch_for: Reserve can read as coldness or disinterest, even when you're fully engaged inside.
Processing privately before responding leaves others guessing; a brief “let me think on that” bridges the gap.
Sharing a little more than feels necessary helps others feel connected to you.
Bringing feeling into the conversation, not just analysis, makes your insight land as warmth, not distance.

conflict.subhead: Conflict Style — Step Back and Analyze — Staying Objective
bullets: Conflict gets approached by detaching, stepping back, and analyzing the situation objectively.
You withdraw to process rather than engaging the emotion in the moment.
You'd rather understand the problem thoroughly than react to the feeling of it.
Emotional intensity from others can feel like an intrusion to be managed at a distance.
working_with: Detaching to stay objective can read as not caring — others may need your presence, not just your analysis.
Withdrawing to process is fine, but saying so out loud keeps the other person from feeling abandoned.
The feeling layer is real even when it's not logical; meeting it matters as much as solving the problem.
The question worth sitting with: am I stepping back to understand, or to avoid being affected?

center.subhead: Coming Back to Center — Coming Back Into the World
bullets: As a Head Center type, you process the world through the mind — thinking, analyzing, anticipating.
The Head Center's organizing emotion is fear, and for Fives it surfaces as the sense that the world will deplete more than you can spare.
Presence, for you, means coming out of the observation tower and into direct, embodied experience.
The goal isn't to think less; it's to live the things you understand, not just understand them.
off_center: Signals: withdrawal, detachment, living in analysis, treating connection as a drain rather than a source.
The return path: engage the body and the moment. Action and presence pull you out of the head's safe remove.
Notice the reflex to compartmentalize and conserve — that's the pattern, gently visible.
Moving toward your security point (Type 8) means decisive, embodied engagement with the world.

comparison.core_motivation: To be capable, self-sufficient, and unintruded upon — protecting limited inner resources.
comparison.focus: Understanding, knowledge, the demands others place on energy and privacy.
comparison.energy: Observing, analyzing, conserving resources, withdrawing to replenish, mastering chosen domains.
comparison.gifts: Perceptive, knowledgeable, self-sufficient, objective, calm, deeply focused.
comparison.challenges: Detached, withholding of energy and self, prone to living in the mind over lived experience.

subtype_sp5.name: Self-Preservation Five
subtype_sp5.tagline: The Castle Defender — privacy and replenishment as refuge
subtype_sp5.narrative:
Self-Preservation Fives make home their refuge — a private place to retreat, replenish, and feel safe from the demands of the world. There may be a concern with having enough supplies and resources, or paradoxically a backpack-light independence with no geographical attachment at all. Either way, the energy goes into managing a small, protected personal world.

SP Fives can present as deeply private and self-sufficient rather than obviously intellectual or detached. The Five quality shows in how they manage their energy and resources in daily life — withdrawing to replenish, minimizing needs — rather than in visible knowledge-seeking. The boundaries around their personal space are firm and rarely explained.

thinking: Attention goes to managing resources and personal space — having enough, staying self-contained.
Plans around replenishment: how to protect energy and retreat when depleted.
Concerned with the practical infrastructure of independence.
feeling: Feelings are kept especially private; the inner world is guarded behind firm boundaries.
Replenishment in solitude is a genuine emotional need, not a preference.
Depletion from too much demand registers as a real threat to wellbeing.
behaving: Makes home a refuge — a private, controlled space for retreat and replenishment.
Minimizes needs and dependence, managing carefully with limited resources.
Maintains firm, rarely-explained boundaries around personal space and time.

shifts: The Five withdrawal turns toward home and replenishment — a protected refuge from demand.
You may look more privately self-sufficient than intellectual — the energy goes into managing your world.
The growing edge is noticing what replenishment requires, and what happens when you don't get it.

subtype_so5.name: Social Five
subtype_so5.tagline: The Professor — connection through expertise and a formal role
subtype_so5.narrative:
Social Fives master the shared symbols, knowledge, and language of their field, often becoming teachers or learned professionals who contribute expertise through a formal role. The role itself preserves their autonomy — it provides a structured, bounded way to engage with the group without the unstructured social demand they find depleting.

SO Fives can look socially competent and engaged through their expertise, which makes the withdrawal hard to spot. It's structural rather than behavioral — the formal role maintains the distance. They may not seem withdrawn at all while remaining, in essence, observers on the sidelines, contributing through knowledge rather than personal connection.

thinking: Attention goes to mastering the shared knowledge and symbols of a field or group.
Engages the group through expertise and ideas rather than personal disclosure.
Uses the formal role as a structured, bounded way to participate.
feeling: Connection happens through shared understanding more than through personal intimacy.
The formal role provides emotional safety — a defined way to belong without exposure.
Unstructured social demand still feels depleting beneath the competent engagement.
behaving: Contributes expertise through a formal role — teacher, specialist, learned professional.
Engages socially through knowledge, which can mask the underlying withdrawal.
Remains an observer on the sidelines even while visibly participating.

shifts: The Five engagement happens through expertise and a defined role — connection at a structured remove.
You may not look withdrawn at all — competent, engaged, contributing through knowledge.
The growing edge is what happens outside the role: the difference between formal engagement and open social life.

subtype_sx5.name: One-to-One Five
subtype_sx5.tagline: The Secret Agent — selective, intense, compartmentalized intimacy (countertype)
subtype_sx5.narrative:
One-to-One Fives share their inner experiences selectively with carefully chosen intimates, seeking a quality of connection that’s rare and trusted. They keep their lives compartmentalized, sharing different parts with different people. Quietly intense and secretive, with high barriers to trust, they look for an ideal merging that most relationships can’t provide.

This is the countertype within Type 5. SX Fives can appear more emotionally available and connected than the classic detached Five — the intensity in their selected relationships is real. But the compartmentalization is rarely visible from outside; others may not realize how much is kept separate, or that the openness they receive is just one carefully chosen room in a larger, guarded house.

thinking: Attention goes to a few intimates and the quality of connection with them.
Compartmentalizes — different people get different parts of them.
Seeks an ideal of merging and trust that ordinary relationships rarely meet.
feeling: Emotional intensity is real in selected relationships — more available than the classic Five.
Trust barriers are high; intimacy is offered selectively and slowly.
The romantic longing for a rare, total connection runs underneath the reserve.
behaving: Shares inner life selectively with a select few, compartmentalizing relationships.
Can appear connected and warm, masking an inner withdrawal.
Quietly intense and secretive, with parts of life few people ever see.

shifts: The Five reserve opens selectively — intense, trusted connection with a chosen few.
You may look more available and connected than the classic Five — the intensity is real.
The growing edge is the compartmentalization: who gets which parts, and what stays separate.

type_6.name: The Questioner

description.worldview: Sixes experience the world as uncertain and potentially threatening — a place where you can't be sure who or what to trust. Anticipating danger, building security, and finding something reliable to stand on is how you manage the underlying anxiety of not knowing what's coming.
description.core_motivation: To be safe, secure, and prepared — managing an underlying anxiety by anticipating threats, testing trust, and seeking something solid to rely on.

thinking.intro: For Sixes, attention goes to what could go wrong and whether things can be trusted. The mind is a vigilant scanner, running scenarios, questioning, and looking for the catch that others miss.
bullets: Attention goes to potential threats — what could go wrong, what's being missed, where the danger is.
Thinking runs scenarios and contingencies, preparing for problems before they arrive.
Trust is tested rather than assumed; authority and information get questioned.
Doubt is a constant companion — including doubt about your own judgment and decisions.
The mind can argue both sides, seeing the case for and against until certainty is elusive.
This vigilance is a real strength: you anticipate problems others walk straight into.
thinking.inquiry: When does your vigilance protect you, and when does it run on its own?

feeling.intro: Sixes live with an undercurrent of anxiety — sometimes quiet, sometimes loud — that colors how they read situations and people. The relationship to fear is central, whether they move away from it or straight at it.
bullets: Anxiety is the baseline feeling — an undercurrent of “what if” that rises and falls with circumstances.
Trust and loyalty run deep once earned; the bond, once real, is fiercely held.
Fear can show as caution and withdrawal, or flip into counterphobic boldness — running at the threat.
Doubt extends inward, producing a recurring uncertainty about your own perceptions.
Reassurance helps but rarely lasts; the anxiety regenerates around the next unknown.
Underneath the vigilance is a longing for something genuinely solid to rest on.
feeling.inquiry: Where does your fear point you toward something true, and where does it just spin?

behaving.intro: Sixes tend to be loyal, responsible, and prepared. Behavior is organized around managing uncertainty — building security, testing reliability, and committing deeply to the people and systems that prove trustworthy.
bullets: Loyal and committed — once trust is earned, you show up reliably and stand by people.
Prepares for problems — planning, troubleshooting, covering the bases others overlook.
Tests trust before extending it; new people and claims get vetted.
Can swing between seeking authority for security and rebelling against it when it fails the test.
Hesitation and second-guessing can delay action while the doubt runs its course.
Your reliability and troubleshooting are genuine gifts — the steady one others count on in a crisis.
behaving.inquiry: Where are you preparing for a problem that may never come?

inquiry_lines: When does your vigilance protect you, and when does it run on its own?
Where does your fear point you toward something true, and where does it just spin?
Where are you preparing for a problem that may never come?

wing_a.body:
The Five wing brings detachment, analysis, and a need for knowledge into the Six. Where the core Six scans for threat, the Five wing adds intellectual depth and a measured, observing quality. Sixes with a Five wing tend to be more reserved, studious, and independent in how they manage uncertainty.

At their best: loyal and insightful — vigilance grounded in clear understanding.

wing_b.body:
The Seven wing brings optimism, energy, and a taste for possibility into the Six. Where the core Six anticipates danger, the Seven wing adds lightness and forward momentum. Sixes with a Seven wing tend to be more outgoing, adventurous, and able to balance caution with enthusiasm.

At their best: loyal and engaging — security-seeking lightened by optimism.

stress.narrative: Under significant pressure, Sixes can shift toward Three energy — becoming driven, image-focused, and busy as a way to outrun the anxiety. Activity substitutes for security; productivity becomes a defense. Noticed early, it's a signal that the underlying fear is being managed by doing rather than addressed.
stress.resource_card: Under pressure: overdrive, image-management, busyness as defense. Consciously accessed: confidence, efficiency, and the ability to act decisively.

security.narrative: When Sixes feel genuinely safe and supported, they move toward Nine energy — becoming more relaxed, trusting, and at ease. The vigilance quiets; there's more room to settle, accept, and let the next unknown simply be unknown.
security.resource_card: In flow: ease, trust, relaxation. Available now: letting the vigilance rest and trusting that things can be okay.

strengths.title: Loyalty and Commitment
strengths.body: A deep, dependable faithfulness to the people and causes you trust — the one who stays when others leave.

strengths.title: Foresight and Preparedness
strengths.body: A talent for anticipating problems and planning for them — the troubleshooter who keeps things from falling apart.

strengths.title: Courage Under Pressure
strengths.body: An ability to act for the group's safety even while afraid — protective, responsible, and steady in a crisis.

challenges.title: Chronic Anxiety
challenges.body: An underlying worry that scans for threat even when none is present — vigilance that exhausts as much as it protects.

challenges.title: Self-Doubt
challenges.body: Difficulty trusting your own judgment — second-guessing decisions and looking outward for certainty that doesn't last.

challenges.title: Suspicion and Testing
challenges.body: A reflex to question motives and test trust that can strain relationships and keep connection at arm's length.

practices.intro: These practices can help you build on what's already working and work with the patterns that can hold you back.
bullets: Distinguish real signal from background noise. Some fears point at genuine problems; many just spin. Learning the difference is the core skill.
Practice trusting your own judgment. Make a small decision and stand by it without seeking outside reassurance — the muscle strengthens with use.
Notice the certainty you're chasing. There's no final guarantee against uncertainty — and acting without one is possible and often necessary.
Let trust extend a little before it's fully earned. Constant testing protects you and also keeps people at a distance.
Practice resting in 'okay.' Moving toward your security point (Type 9) means letting the vigilance set down and trusting the moment.

communication.subhead: Communication Style — Questioning, Careful, and Loyal
bullets: You communicate with care and thoroughness — raising concerns, asking the questions others skip.
You test ideas and people, probing for what might be missing or untrustworthy.
You can argue multiple sides, which makes you fair but can read as ambivalent.
Your loyalty comes through once trust is established — you advocate hard for your people.
watch_for: Raising what could go wrong, however useful, can land as negativity if it's all the other person hears.
Questioning trust can feel like suspicion to the person being questioned; naming your intent softens it.
Your ambivalence can confuse others; stating where you actually land helps them act.
Letting appreciation through, alongside the caution, keeps the vigilance from reading as distrust.

conflict.subhead: Conflict Style — Brace and Engage — Intensity
bullets: Conflict activates the threat-scanner — the stakes and dangers register sharply and fast.
You may brace for the worst, anticipating how things could escalate or who can't be trusted.
Fear can show as withdrawal and caution, or flip into counterphobic confrontation.
Loyalty shapes the response: you defend your people and your principles fiercely.
working_with: The anticipated worst case is often worse than the reality; naming the actual fear shrinks it.
Counterphobic boldness can overshoot — running at a threat that didn't need a charge.
Testing whether the other person is 'with you or against you' can turn an ally into an opponent.
The question worth sitting with: am I responding to a real threat, or to the anxiety about one?

center.subhead: Coming Back to Center — Finding Solid Ground Within
bullets: As a Head Center type, you process the world through the mind — anticipating, scanning, planning.
The Head Center's organizing emotion is fear, and for Sixes it's the most central and active of all.
Presence, for you, means finding inner authority — trusting your own ground rather than scanning for external certainty.
The goal isn't to stop being prepared; it's to act from steadiness rather than from spinning anxiety.
off_center: Signals: scanning for threat, second-guessing, seeking reassurance, the mind running worst cases.
The return path: come into the body and the present. The anxiety lives in the future; the ground is here, now.
Notice the search for outside certainty — that's the pattern, gently visible. The authority you want is inner.
Moving toward your security point (Type 9) means letting the vigilance rest into trust and ease.

comparison.core_motivation: To be safe, secure, and prepared — managing anxiety by anticipating threat and finding what's reliable.
comparison.focus: What could go wrong, whether things can be trusted, sources of security and danger.
comparison.energy: Scanning, planning, testing trust, troubleshooting, committing to trusted people and systems.
comparison.gifts: Loyal, responsible, prepared, perceptive about danger, courageous for the group.
comparison.challenges: Anxious, self-doubting, suspicious, prone to testing trust and chasing unreachable certainty.

subtype_sp6.name: Self-Preservation Six
subtype_sp6.tagline: The Family Loyalist — security through warmth and alliance (countertype-adjacent)
subtype_sp6.narrative:
Self-Preservation Sixes overcome fear by making connections and agreements with people, using personal warmth to build alliances and disarm potential threats. Family — biological or chosen — is the priority, and they invest deeply in a circle of trusted relationships. The warmth is both genuine care and a way of securing safety: friends are less dangerous than strangers.

SP Sixes can present as warm and relational rather than obviously anxious, which makes the fear underneath easy to miss. The disarming quality of the warmth isn't always visible as anxiety management. They can look like Type Twos in their care for close relationships — the difference is that the warmth is, at root, a strategy for safety in an uncertain world.

thinking: Attention goes to building trusted alliances — who's safe, who's family, who can be relied on.
Scans for security through relationship rather than through confrontation or analysis alone.
Hesitation and caution show up around the unfamiliar and the unproven.
feeling: Warmth is genuine and also protective — connection lowers the threat of an uncertain world.
Anxiety is present but softened by the security of trusted bonds.
Fear of taking risks or stepping outside known boundaries runs underneath the friendliness.
behaving: Builds warm, loyal relationships and prioritizes family — biological or chosen.
Uses personal warmth to disarm others and create a circle of safety.
Stays within well-known boundaries; new and uncertain situations bring caution.

shifts: The Six fear is managed through warmth and alliance — safety built through trusted relationships.
You may look like a warm Two, the anxiety hidden beneath the friendliness and care.
The growing edge is seeing the warmth's protective function — and what happens when you don't know where you stand.

subtype_so6.name: Social Six
subtype_so6.tagline: The Social Guardian — security through duty, roles, and the rules
subtype_so6.narrative:
Social Sixes take responsibility for the agenda and security of the group. Having a clear role and clear rules is a primary concern — they need to know the guidelines, or to create them, in order to feel safe and avoid the rejection that comes with getting it wrong. They provide real service through their ability to organize and structure things for everyone’s benefit.

SO Sixes can look like highly engaged institutional loyalists — often the people who make the system work. The anxiety gets channeled into the role, which can make them resemble Type Ones (rule-following) or Type Threes (responsible achievers). The duty is genuine, but it can also become a burden that has them set aside their own needs and feelings.

thinking: Attention goes to the group’s rules, roles, and agenda and whether the guidelines are clear.
Seeks safety through structure, trusting that systems and processes reduce threat.
Tracks where they stand with the group and whether they’re meeting expectations.
feeling: Security comes from a clear role and clear rules; ambiguity raises the anxiety sharply.
Duty is felt deeply — and can become a burden that crowds out their own needs.
Fear of rejection drives the responsible, by-the-book engagement.
behaving: Takes responsibility for the group — organizing, structuring, carrying out social duty reliably.
Needs to know the rules to feel safe and avoid dangerous scenarios.
Can look like a rule-following One or a responsible SP Three.

shifts: The Six fear is managed through duty and structure — safety found in clear roles and rules.
You may look like a dutiful One or a responsible Three, the anxiety channeled into the role.
The growing edge is what happens when the rules aren't clear — and the personal feelings the duty crowds out.

subtype_sx6.name: One-to-One Six
subtype_sx6.tagline: The Warrior — fear met head-on with strength and boldness (countertype)
subtype_sx6.narrative:
One-to-One Sixes demonstrate a warrior spirit — overcoming fear through willpower, physical or intellectual strength, and fierce, often ideological positions. This is the counterphobic stance: rather than retreating from fear, they run straight at it, taking risks and confronting threats to prove the fear won’t rule them.

This is the countertype of Type 6, and it can look strikingly like a Type Eight — confrontational, risk-taking, ideologically intense, apparently fearless. But the fear is present underneath, carefully hidden, sometimes even from the Six themselves. The boldness is about pushing against their fear, not the absence of it.

thinking: Attention goes to confronting threats directly — running at fear rather than away from it.
Holds strong, often ideological positions as a source of strength and certainty.
The vigilance is still scanning, but the response is to charge rather than retreat.
feeling: Fear is met counterphobically — pushed against with willpower and force rather than avoided.
The boldness is anti-fear behavior; the anxiety is present but hidden, even from themselves.
Under sustained pressure, the underlying fear surfaces beneath the strength.
behaving: Confronts threats head-on — risk-taking, bold, fiercely committed to positions and people.
Channels fear into strength, intensity, or the creation of beauty and stability.
Can look strikingly like a Type Eight — direct, forceful, apparently fearless.

shifts: The Six fear is met head-on — willpower and boldness pushing straight against the threat.
You may be mistaken for an Eight: confrontational, risk-taking, seemingly without fear.
The growing edge is recognizing the fear beneath the boldness — present even as you fight it.

type_7.name: The Enthusiast

description.worldview: Sevens experience the world as a place full of exciting possibilities — and pain, limitation, and boredom as things to be avoided. Staying open to options, keeping things positive, and moving toward the next stimulating experience is how you stay free and ahead of discomfort.
description.core_motivation: To be happy, free, and satisfied — staying open to possibility and pleasure while avoiding pain, limitation, and the discomfort of being trapped.

thinking.intro: For Sevens, attention goes to options, possibilities, and what's interesting next. The mind is quick, associative, and future-oriented — synthesizing ideas and reframing the negative into the positive.
bullets: Attention goes to possibilities and options — what's exciting, what's next, what could be.
Thinking is fast and associative, jumping between ideas and connecting them in novel ways.
The mind reframes the negative into the positive almost automatically.
Keeping options open feels essential; commitment can register as limitation and loss.
Planning the pleasurable future is more engaging than staying with the present.
This quick, optimistic mind is a real gift — and it can also outrun depth and follow-through.
thinking.inquiry: What are you keeping your options open to avoid choosing?

feeling.intro: Sevens gravitate toward positive emotion and away from pain. The quick pivot to the next good thing keeps life enjoyable — and can also be a way of staying ahead of feelings that would slow them down.
bullets: Positive feeling is the comfort zone; pain and difficulty get reframed or moved past quickly.
Enthusiasm and appetite are genuine — there's real joy and energy in engagement.
Difficult emotions get outrun rather than felt — the pivot to the next thing is fast.
Underneath the optimism can be a fear of being trapped in pain with no way out.
Boredom and limitation feel genuinely threatening, not just unpleasant.
Staying with a hard feeling, rather than escaping it, is the growing edge and the doorway to depth.
feeling.inquiry: What feeling are you moving fast enough to stay ahead of?

behaving.intro: Sevens tend to be energetic, spontaneous, and engaging. Behavior is organized around keeping life stimulating — pursuing experiences, generating plans, and keeping the exits open.
bullets: Energetic and spontaneous — pursuing experiences, generating ideas, keeping life full and moving.
Keeps options open, sometimes overcommitting to possibilities and under-delivering on follow-through.
Reframes constraints and avoids being pinned down or bored.
Can scatter across too many interests, with depth and completion losing out to breadth.
Moves quickly past discomfort — in conversations, situations, and feelings alike.
The energy and optimism genuinely lift others — the work is staying long enough to go deep.
behaving.inquiry: Where would staying put, even when it's boring, actually serve you?

inquiry_lines: What are you keeping your options open to avoid choosing?
What feeling are you moving fast enough to stay ahead of?
Where would staying put, even when it's boring, actually serve you?

wing_a.body:
The Six wing brings caution, loyalty, and a sense of responsibility into the Seven. Where the core Seven keeps options open, the Six wing adds commitment and an awareness of risk. Sevens with a Six wing tend to be more grounded, relational, and willing to follow through on what they start.

At their best: enthusiastic and committed — possibility balanced with loyalty and follow-through.

wing_b.body:
The Eight wing brings assertiveness, drive, and intensity into the Seven. Where the core Seven seeks pleasure and possibility, the Eight wing adds force and a willingness to take charge. Sevens with an Eight wing tend to be more bold, ambitious, and entrepreneurial, pursuing what they want with directness.

At their best: enthusiastic and powerful — vision driven into reality with force.

stress.narrative: Under significant pressure, Sevens can shift toward One energy — becoming critical, rigid, and perfectionistic. The easy optimism narrows into frustration, judgment, and a sharp focus on what's wrong. Noticed early, it's a signal that the avoidance of pain has finally caught up.
stress.resource_card: Under pressure: criticism, rigidity, frustration. Consciously accessed: discernment, focus, and the discipline to finish what matters.

security.narrative: When Sevens feel genuinely safe and supported, they move toward Five energy — becoming more focused, reflective, and able to go deep rather than wide. The scattered breadth gives way to sustained attention; possibility settles into genuine mastery.
security.resource_card: In flow: depth, focus, sustained attention. Available now: trading breadth for genuine depth and mastery in what matters.

strengths.title: Optimism and Energy
strengths.body: An infectious enthusiasm and zest for life that lifts the people around you and makes hard things feel possible.

strengths.title: Quick, Synthesizing Mind
strengths.body: A fast, creative intelligence that connects ideas, generates possibilities, and sees opportunity where others see dead ends.

strengths.title: Adaptable Resilience
strengths.body: An ability to bounce back, reframe setbacks, and keep moving forward — finding the upside and the next open door.

challenges.title: Avoidance of Pain
challenges.body: A reflex to escape difficulty and discomfort — outrunning the feelings and situations that depth requires staying with.

challenges.title: Scattered Focus
challenges.body: Spreading across too many interests and options — breadth and momentum at the cost of depth and completion.

challenges.title: Fear of Commitment
challenges.body: Keeping the exits open to avoid being trapped — which can leave relationships and projects perpetually unfinished.

practices.intro: These practices can help you build on what's already working and work with the patterns that can hold you back.
bullets: Practice staying with discomfort instead of pivoting. The feeling you move past holds the depth you're actually looking for.
Notice the reframe in real time. The automatic positive spin is a gift — and sometimes it skips a truth worth facing.
Choose depth over breadth on purpose. Committing to one thing fully — and finishing it — delivers a satisfaction that options never do.
Treat commitment as freedom, not a trap. The open door you keep can be the very thing keeping you from arriving anywhere.
Cultivate focus and stillness. Moving toward your security point (Type 5) means going deep, sitting with one thing long enough to master it.

communication.subhead: Communication Style — Quick, Engaging, and Possibility-Focused
bullets: You communicate with energy and enthusiasm — engaging, idea-rich, and fun to be around.
You connect ideas quickly and generate possibilities, sometimes faster than others can track.
You reframe toward the positive and keep the conversation moving and light.
You may skip past the hard or heavy parts, steering toward what's more enjoyable.
watch_for: The fast pace can leave others behind; slowing to let them catch up makes the energy land as connection.
Reframing pain too quickly can leave people feeling unheard — sometimes the hard thing needs to be sat with, not solved.
Following one thread to its end, rather than jumping, gives your ideas room to deepen.
Letting a serious moment stay serious builds the trust that constant lightness can't.

conflict.subhead: Conflict Style — Reframe and Redirect — Keeping It Positive
bullets: Conflict feels like a trap and a source of pain, so the instinct is to lighten, reframe, or escape it.
You may pivot to the positive or to a new option rather than staying in the difficulty.
Direct, heavy confrontation is uncomfortable — better to find the upside or the exit.
The avoidance can leave real issues unaddressed while everyone stays superficially upbeat.
working_with: Reframing conflict away doesn't resolve it — the unaddressed issue waits and often grows.
The pivot to positivity can feel dismissive to someone who needs their difficulty acknowledged.
Staying in the discomfort long enough to actually resolve it is the harder, more rewarding path.
The question worth sitting with: am I resolving this, or just escaping the discomfort of it?

center.subhead: Coming Back to Center — Coming Down Into the Present
bullets: As a Head Center type, you process the world through the mind — planning, imagining, anticipating what's next.
The Head Center's organizing emotion is fear, and for Sevens it surfaces as the fear of being trapped in pain.
Presence, for you, means landing in the present moment rather than living in the planned-for future.
The goal isn't to lose your optimism; it's to be here fully, including for the parts that aren't fun.
off_center: Signals: restlessness, scattered focus, planning the next thing, an itch to move on or escape.
The return path: slow down and arrive. Staying with one thing, one moment, pulls you out of the future-mind.
Notice the reframe and the pivot in real time — that's the pattern, gently visible.
Moving toward your security point (Type 5) means depth, focus, and the willingness to stay.

comparison.core_motivation: To be happy, free, and satisfied — pursuing possibility and pleasure while avoiding pain and limitation.
comparison.focus: Options, possibilities, what's interesting next, the pleasurable future, escape routes from discomfort.
comparison.energy: Pursuing experiences, generating ideas, reframing the negative, keeping options open and moving.
comparison.gifts: Optimistic, energetic, quick-thinking, adaptable, joyful, a synthesizer of ideas.
comparison.challenges: Pain-avoidant, scattered, commitment-shy, prone to breadth over depth and unfinished pursuits.

subtype_sp7.name: Self-Preservation Seven
subtype_sp7.tagline: The Epicure — abundance and pleasure within a trusted circle
subtype_sp7.narrative:
Self-Preservation Sevens create an abundant lifestyle within their family and circle of friends — good food, good conversation, fun projects, and a network of opportunities and pleasures. This is the classic epicurean Seven, with a real gift for entrepreneurial ventures and for keeping interesting options alive within a known, trusted world.

Of the three Seven subtypes, this one is closest to the classic Seven stereotype, so it's often recognized readily. What can be missed is the self-preservation element — the focus on a safe, abundant personal world rather than wide social expansion. The “family” orientation toward a known circle can even look Two-like or Six-like in its focus on a chosen few.

thinking: Attention goes to creating abundance and opportunity within a trusted circle of family and friends.
Networks practically — keeping good options, connections, and pleasures alive.
Plans for an enjoyable, well-stocked personal world rather than wide social expansion.
feeling: Genuine appetite and warmth for the pleasures of a good life shared with a known circle.
Comfort and abundance soothe the underlying fear of limitation.
An undercurrent of wanting to secure enough — enough good things, enough good people.
behaving: Builds an abundant lifestyle — good food, good company, fun projects, practical networks.
Often entrepreneurial, keeping interesting options and opportunities in play.
Focuses on a known, trusted circle rather than broad social reach.

shifts: The Seven appetite turns toward a trusted circle — abundance and pleasure in a known, secure world.
You may look like the classic Seven, with a self-preserving focus on your own good life that's easy to miss.
The growing edge is the preservative pull — what happens when the comfort or pleasure feels threatened.

subtype_so7.name: Social Seven
subtype_so7.tagline: The Social Visionary — pleasure sacrificed in service of a shared ideal (countertype)
subtype_so7.narrative:
Social Sevens sacrifice some of their own gluttonous desires in service of the group or a social ideal. To keep their place and belong, they accept limits they would otherwise resist, channeling their expansive energy into visions for a better world. There's idealism here, and a willingness to give up immediate pleasure for a larger purpose.

This is the countertype within Type 7, and it doesn't look like the indulgent or scattered Seven at all. SO Sevens can resemble Type Twos because of their service orientation and their acceptance of personal limits to support others and causes. The gluttony is sublimated into social idealism — but the relationship to their own pleasure remains complicated, often carrying guilt or expressed only through service.

thinking: Attention goes to a social vision or ideal — a better future the group could move toward.
Weighs personal desire against the group's good, accepting limits to belong and contribute.
Channels expansive energy into purpose rather than personal indulgence.
feeling: Idealism and a sense of contribution take precedence over immediate personal pleasure.
A complicated relationship to enjoyment — sometimes guilt, sometimes pleasure routed through service.
The underlying fear of limitation is met by sacrificing for something larger.
behaving: Sacrifices personal desires for the group or cause — accepting limits in service of an ideal.
Can look like a service-oriented Two rather than an indulgent Seven.
Directs energy into visions for a better world and into contribution.

shifts: The Seven appetite is sublimated into a social ideal — pleasure given up in service of something larger.
You may be mistaken for a Two: service-oriented, self-limiting, anything but indulgent.
The growing edge is the relationship to your own pleasure — what you do purely for your own delight.

subtype_sx7.name: One-to-One Seven
subtype_sx7.tagline: The Adventurer — enthusiasm idealized and channeled into fascination
subtype_sx7.narrative:
One-to-One Sevens are dreamers — easily influenced by the attraction of new ideas, adventures, and relationships, and gifted with great powers of suggestion. They use their charm to lead others into new paradigms, purchases, and possibilities, and they idealize the people and experiences they’re fascinated by, seeing the world through optimistic, rose-colored possibility.

The suggestibility works both ways: SX Sevens can appear as followers, easily pulled into others’ plans, or as leaders, pulling others into theirs. The quick direction changes can look like Type Four or Type Eight depending on the day. The fascination is real but tends to move — satiated with one possibility, they’re drawn to the next.

thinking: Attention goes to pleasurable possibilities — the fascinating idea, person, or adventure.
Highly suggestible and highly suggestive, fascinated by fresh perspectives.
Sees through rose-colored optimism, idealizing what’s caught their fascination.
feeling: Enthusiasm runs high and to others can feel like infectious energy.
The intensity tends to move; satiation with one possibility automatically leads to the next.
Underneath the optimism is the Seven’s avoidance of limitation and pain.
behaving: Chases fascination — new adventures and relationships are pursued with verve.
Changes directions quickly, pivoting towards what's more pleasing or fascinating.
Has a hard time sticking with one thing or one direction.

shifts: The Seven appetite concentrates into fascination — idealized people, ideas, and adventures.
You may be mistaken for a Four (in the idealizing) or an Eight (in the impulsivity), depending on the day.
The growing edge is what sustains enthusiasm over time — the commitments that have actually lasted.
